docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Use the smallest test that covers your change, then run the broader checks before opening a pull request.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
npm run lint
npm run type-check
npm test
npm run compile

npm test runs the unit tests. The pretest step also checks that the ipcraft-spec submodule is available. If it is missing, run:

git submodule update --init --recursive

docs.title: Choose the right test
docs.text: Change Start with Also run Algorithm, parser, service, or utility npm test npm run type-check React component or editor interaction npm test npm run test:browser Extension host or VS Code command npm run compile npm run test:e2e Generator template or HDL output npm run test:integration:hdl Relevant vendor test Documentation only mkdocs build --strict Link and spelling review

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
Unit tests use Jest and cover pure functions, services, and React components. The Jest configuration is not in the repository root, so always pass it when running one file or one named test:

npx jest --config config/jest.config.js src/test/suite/services/YamlValidator.test.ts
npx jest --config config/jest.config.js -t "should parse valid YAML"

Run the complete unit suite with:

npm test

Tests use the shared VS Code mock in __mocks__/vscode.ts. Extend that mock when a test needs another VS Code API. Do not create a separate mock in each test file.

docs.title: Browser tests
docs.text:
Browser tests use Playwright to exercise the Memory Map and IP Core webviews without starting VS Code:

npm run compile
npm run test:browser

The test harness passes YAML to the webview through window.__RENDER__. Use browser tests for keyboard navigation, drag behavior, focus, and other interactions that depend on a real browser.

docs.title: VS Code tests
docs.text:
These tests start a real VS Code Extension Development Host:

npm run compile
npm run test:e2e

Use them for extension activation, command registration, custom editors, and behavior that depends on VS Code itself.

docs.title: HDL integration tests
docs.text:
These tests generate HDL and compile it with GHDL or Icarus Verilog:

npm run test:integration:hdl

Use this suite after changing schemas, generator logic, or HDL templates.

docs.title: Vendor integration tests
docs.text:
Vendor tests validate generated Quartus and Vivado projects:

npm run test:integration:quartus
npm run test:integration:vivado

These tests need the matching vendor tools or configured container support. See Run the EDA integration tests.

docs.title: Where tests live
docs.text: Test type Location Environment Unit and React tests src/test/suite/ Jest with jsdom VS Code tests src/test/e2e/ VS Code Extension Host Browser tests src/test/browser/ Playwright HDL and vendor tests src/test/integration/ Node plus external tools Shared test inputs src/test/fixtures/ YAML and generated examples

docs.title: Writing a test
docs.text:
1. Put the test in the suite that matches the environment it needs.
  2. Use the smallest input that demonstrates the behavior.
  3. Check the visible result or written document, not an internal detail.
  4. Add a regression test when fixing a bug.
  5. Run the focused test before running the full suite.

For browser tests, prefer stable roles and labels over CSS implementation details. For generator tests, check meaningful output and compile it when possible.

docs.title: The submodule is missing
docs.text: git submodule update --init --recursive

docs.title: Browser tests use an old bundle
docs.text:
Rebuild before running Playwright:

npm run compile
npm run test:browser

docs.title: A VS Code test cannot find compiled files
docs.text: Run npm run compile first. These tests load compiled output, not TypeScript source files.

docs.title: A mock works once and then disappears
docs.text: Jest resets mock implementations between tests. Restore the implementation in beforeEach.

docs.title: Jest collects the wrong files
docs.text: Use --config config/jest.config.js. Browser tests use Playwright, and VS Code tests use their own runner.

docs.title: Before opening a pull request
docs.text:
npm run lint
npm run type-check
npm test
npm run compile

Then run the browser, VS Code, HDL, or vendor suites that cover the changed area. In the pull request, state which commands you ran and note any suite you could not run locally.

docs.title: Bit Field Handling
docs.text:
This page explains how IPCraft stores, displays, moves, and saves register bit fields. It is intended for contributors changing the Memory Map editor.

For keyboard commands and function names, see the bit field interaction reference.

docs.title: Core rule
docs.text:
The bits value in the memory-map document is the saved source of truth. For example, "7:4" means a four-bit field covering bits 7 through 4.

The editor derives three temporary views from that value:

  • table rows for editing names, access, reset values, and positions;
  • visual segments for drawing the register;
  • a bit-ownership array for pointer interactions.

Temporary row IDs, selected cells, and unfinished text edits are editor state. They must never be written to YAML.

docs.title: Main modules
docs.text:
Responsibility Main module Calculate positions src/webview/algorithms/LayoutEngine.ts Insert into free space src/webview/services/SpatialInsertionService.ts Apply field operations src/webview/services/FieldOperationService.ts Edit field rows src/webview/hooks/useFieldEditor.ts Draw fields and gaps src/webview/components/bitfield/ Commit YAML changes src/webview/hooks/useYamlUpdateHandler.ts Preserve row identity src/webview/utils/rowIdentity.ts

Keep position calculations in LayoutEngine.ts. Components and hooks should request a layout change, not calculate one themselves.

docs.title: Two layout operations
docs.text: IPCraft deliberately uses two different rules.

docs.title: Insert or delete: close all gaps
docs.text: recomputeBitfieldLayout(fields, regWidth) places fields next to each other from bit 0 upward. It is used after a structural change such as insertion or deletion.

docs.title: Move: keep existing gaps
docs.text:
reorderBitfieldLayout(fields, movedIdx, direction, regWidth) swaps a field with the next field in the requested direction. Empty space between fields is kept.

This makes a move predictable: the chosen field changes place, but unrelated parts of the register do not shift.

docs.title: Field order
docs.text:
The field array is stored from the highest bit to the lowest bit. The table and visualizer use the same order.

After an operation:

  1. every field must remain inside the register width;
  2. fields must not overlap;
  3. array order must match bit order;
  4. saved bits values must match the displayed positions.

Reject an invalid change before writing it to the document.

docs.title: Insert, delete, and move
docs.text:
A structural gesture must result in one document update. Do not send one update for the array change and another for recalculated positions. Two updates can be processed against different document versions and leave the file inconsistent.

Field moves use the special path ['__op', 'field-move']. The update handler passes that operation to FieldOperationService, which calls the layout engine and writes the complete result.

docs.title: Editing the Bits cell
docs.text:
The Bits cell accepts either a single bit such as 3 or a range such as 7:4. While the user types, the editor keeps a draft string so incomplete input is not immediately written to YAML.

The cell follows these rules:

  • valid committed input updates the field and any affected neighbors;
  • invalid or overlapping input is rejected;
  • Escape restores the value from the document;
  • an external document update replaces a stale draft, even while focused;
  • the displayed range always follows the normalized field value.

Direct position edits may move neighboring fields to keep the layout valid. The change follows array order and remains within the current register.

docs.title: Selection after an operation
docs.text:
Selection uses the field's stable rowId, not its old array index. This lets focus follow a field after rows are reordered.

Keyboard and mouse insertion have different focus behavior:

  • keyboard insertion selects the new row but keeps focus at table level;
  • mouse insertion selects the row and opens the first editable cell.

Calling focusCellEditor after keyboard insertion makes later table shortcuts look like text input. Keep the two paths separate.

docs.title: Document synchronization
docs.text:
Every edit includes the document version it was based on. The extension rejects an edit based on an older version and sends the current document back to the webview.

The webview also ignores echoes of its own completed edits. This prevents an older render from replacing a newer local state.

The paired implementation is in:

  • src/services/WebviewRouter.ts on the extension side;
  • src/webview/sync/revisionFilter.ts on the webview side.

Change and test these two modules together.

docs.title: Saved positions remain authoritative
docs.text: Positions are part of the memory-map format and affect generated hardware. They cannot be reconstructed from row order alone because valid documents may contain gaps.

docs.title: Layout calculations are pure
docs.text: The layout engine receives fields and returns fields. It does not access React, VS Code, or the file system. This makes the rules easier to test.

docs.title: Commits are atomic
docs.text: One gesture produces one complete document change. This protects the revision protocol and makes undo behave as the user expects.

docs.title: Row identity is not document data
docs.text: rowId exists only to keep React rows stable. Serialization removes it along with other editor-only properties.

docs.title: Tests to run
docs.text:
Changes to bit-field behavior should cover:

  • layout calculations and boundary cases;
  • insertion into gaps and full registers;
  • move behavior with and without gaps;
  • direct Bits-cell edits and invalid drafts;
  • keyboard and pointer focus behavior;
  • serialization without rowId or other editor-only values;
  • stale update and echo filtering.

Run the focused Jest test first, then the complete unit suite and browser tests:

npm test
npm run compile
npm run test:browser

docs.title: Diagram renderer
docs.text: src/shared/render/ turns a laid-out diagram into a standalone SVG without a browser. It backs ipcraft render and the interactive Export image of the system viewer and the IP core editor (issue #268), so an image looks the same whichever way it was made. It draws whole system levels and IP core symbols.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
The module is pure and runs in Node and in a browser: no DOM, no React, no CSS and no file access. It sits above the pure layout code and below the callers:

domain, layout (src/webview/systemDiagram/layout, legend.ts, model.ts)
  -> src/shared/render
  -> src/cli/render.ts (reads files, runs the layout, writes the SVG)

It imports only DOM-free layout and model modules from the system diagram, and canvas/canvasLayout.ts from the IP core canvas. Fonts come in as bytes (fontFaceCss), so the renderer never reads files. The CLI bundle has no .css loader: nothing on the render path may import CSS, React or @xyflow/react at runtime (layout/nodeHandles.ts keeps its own Position values for that reason).

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Module Responsibility systemLevelSvg.ts renderSystemLevelSvg: document, background, grid, draw order, legend placement blockSvg.ts Instance blocks and expanded frames: header, subtitle, hierarchy toggle, pin rows pinSvg.ts Pin markers, net badges, external port tags legendSvg.ts Legend layout (wrapping rows) and drawing ipSymbolSvg.ts renderIpSymbolSvg: IP core symbol document, block header and sections, bounds, grid ipPortSvg.ts IP symbol ports: stubs, dots, icons, badges, collapsed bus bundles palette.ts Light and Dark colors; mixSrgb textMetrics.ts, fontMetrics.generated.ts IBM Plex text measurement, baselines, truncation fontFaces.ts Base64 @font-face rules for the three WOFF files woffToSfnt.ts WOFF 1.0 to TrueType unwrapping, for the rasterizer raster.ts rasterize: SVG to PNG or JPG (resvg-wasm, jpeg-js) svg.ts, textSvg.ts Escaping, number formatting, one-line text

docs.title: Palette
docs.text: palette.ts is the TypeScript source of truth for the colors of exported images. The webview resolves --vscode-* tokens at run time; an image has no theme, so the same tokens are pinned to the Light Modern and Dark Modern values copied from scripts/docs-screenshots/theme/. Roles the webview derives with color-mix (--sd-node-line, --sd-node-fill, --sd-node-head-fill, resting wires) are computed with mixSrgb using the same formulas. When a color changes in systemDiagram.css or colors.ts, change the palette too; Palette.ip mirrors canvas.css the same way. The charts blue, orange and yellow come from the VS Code color registry defaults (Light Modern and Dark Modern do not override them). No palette value contains var(.

docs.title: Text and fonts
docs.text: Text is drawn in IBM Plex Sans (400, 600) and IBM Plex Mono (400), measured with their advance widths. fontMetrics.generated.ts is written by npm run generate:font-metrics from the @fontsource devDependencies with fontkit; fontkit never runs at runtime. The SVG sets font-kerning: none and text-rendering: geometricPrecision (without it Chrome on Linux rounds every glyph advance to a whole pixel and measured text overflows its block), so drawn widths equal measured widths. plexTextMeasure is the TextMeasure the layout uses in Node, with the webview's weights (11 px body, 12 px semibold, 10.5 px mono). Characters outside the table are measured as M. The WOFF (1.0) files are copied to dist/resources/fonts/ (ResourceRoots.fontsDir) and allow-listed in scripts/check-vsix.js and scripts/prepare-cli-package.js.

docs.title: Differences from the canvas
docs.text: The canvas styling lives in systemDiagram.css; the renderer mirrors it in code. Deliberate simplifications are listed in the systemLevelSvg.ts header: no shadows, user highlight colors, dimming, review or selected clock tree; the legend sits below the drawing; grid dots are slightly larger for print. Output is deterministic: numbers have at most two decimals and elements follow the layout order (frames, wires, blocks, legend).

docs.title: Decorations
docs.text:
renderSystemLevelSvg draws what the layout carries plus two optional inputs, and without them its output is byte-identical to an undecorated render.

  • Selection. selectedNodeIds draws the viewer's selected style (focus color outline; data-selected="true" on the node group). The CLI passes the --select and --highlight nodes (cli/renderSystemOptions.ts). --select isolates with hopDistances, isolationSubset and maxRadius and passes the subset to buildElkInput as isolate, as useElkLayout does.
  • Clocks and resets. clockDecor (domain mode) and applyClockDecor merge the domain strips, pin marks and wire marks into the node and edge data, with clockNodeData, the same function useCanvasElements uses. The renderer reads them from the data: decorSvg.ts draws the strip, header count, frequency labels and selection ring; blockSvg.ts and pinSvg.ts color the markers and crossing pins; systemLevelSvg.ts dashes crossing wires in the warning color and fades the other data wires; legendSvg.ts appends the domainLegend entries. Domain colors are CSS variables in the webview; resolveColor maps them through Palette.tokens. Frequency labels get a halo in the background color, like the viewer's text shadow.

docs.title: IP core symbol
docs.text:
renderIpSymbolSvg(layout, options) draws what the IP core editor's canvas shows in its default state from a CanvasLayout. The geometry is not recomputed: the layout comes from computeLayout in canvas/canvasLayout.ts, called through computeSymbolLayout in canvas/symbolInputs.ts, the pure module that also builds the bus-library lookups, protocol labels and clock-domain colors for IpBlockCanvas.tsx, so the canvas and the CLI cannot drift. IpBlockDiagram.tsx and the Canvas* components cannot be imported (they load React and the webview host), so ipSymbolSvg.ts and ipPortSvg.ts mirror their geometry and canvas.css styles by hand; change both together. Colors are Palette.ip. The IP canvas colors clocks green and resets orange, while the system diagram colors them orange and red; both are kept as the editors draw them.

src/cli/renderIpCore.ts reads the file (yaml parse, format version check, canonicalizeParsedIpCore), loads the built-in bus library plus the file's useBusLibrary folder, and writes the SVG. Simplifications are listed in the ipSymbolSvg.ts header: no selection, hover, rename or validation marks, bus bundles always collapsed, no drop shadow, the canvas margin cropped to 24 px around the drawing, and small native shapes in place of the glyphs the embedded fonts lack.

docs.title: PNG and JPG
docs.text:
rasterize (raster.ts) draws the same SVG with @resvg/resvg-wasm: the wasm module is initialized once per process from bytes the caller reads (ResourceRoots.resvgWasmPath, dist/resources/resvg.wasm), so the glue never fetches or resolves a URL, which keeps it bundleable into dist/cli.js. The zoom is --scale; PNG is resvg's asPng(), JPG is its RGBA pixels through jpeg-js (no alpha, so the drawing, system level or IP symbol, is flattened onto the palette background; a transparent JPG is rejected by the parser). Output is deterministic.

resvg ignores CSS @font-face and does not read WOFF or WOFF2, so the CLI passes the same three shipped WOFF files through woffToSfnt (Node's zlib.inflateSync as the inflate function) and gives resvg the TrueType bytes; system fonts are off. One shipped format therefore serves both outputs. Known differences from a browser:

  • Semibold sans text names the family 'IBM Plex Sans SemiBold', 'IBM Plex Sans', sans-serif (SANS_SEMIBOLD_FAMILY), because resvg matches the family name table of the TrueType file, which for the 600 face is "IBM Plex Sans SemiBold". The SVGs define no @font-face of that name, so a browser uses the embedded 'IBM Plex Sans' at weight 600, or a locally installed 'IBM Plex Sans SemiBold' (the same design) if there is one.
  • resvg does not synthesize bold, so any text the SVG asks for in bold uses the regular face (IBM Plex Mono ships only at 400; Sans has real 400 and 600 faces).
  • It does not apply font-kerning or text-rendering hints, and its glyph rasterization (anti-aliasing, hinting) differs slightly from Chrome's, so pixels are not identical to a screenshot of the webview.

docs.title: Workspace definitions and manifests
docs.text:
ipcraft render of a system design runs the same enrichment as the viewer, so an image shows the pins the viewer shows. The pipeline is one function, enrichSystemGraph (src/services/systemDiagram/enrichment/): subsystem grafting (expandSubsystems), matchDefinitions, definitionFromIpCore and definitionFromHdl, applyDefinitions. It does no I/O of its own: the caller passes an EnrichmentIo (the three file lists and readText) and an optional logger. There are two adapters:

Adapter Files Extras SystemDesignEnricher, SubsystemExpander WorkspaceFileIndex over vscode.workspace.findFiles, watchers trust check src/cli/workspaceIo.ts sorted fs walk of --workspace lists cached per directory for the process

Both build index entries with the pure fileEntries.ts, so matching, the HDL size cap and the entity/module scan cannot differ. enrichSystemGraph stays below the CLI and the extension in the dependency order.

--manifest (cli/renderManifest.ts) renders a list of images in one process. renderManifestSpec.ts converts an entry, with the manifest defaults underneath, into the argv of the equivalent ipcraft render call and parseRenderArgs validates it, so flags and manifest keys share one set of rules. A RenderSession holds what is loaded once for the batch: fonts, bus libraries per useBusLibrary folder and the workspace file lists; the wasm rasterizer is already once per process.

docs.title: Shared render service
docs.text:
src/services/render/ is the Node-side service both callers use, so neither duplicates the layout, drawing or encoding steps:

Module Responsibility systemLevelImage.ts renderSystemLevelImage(graph, request, look, encoding, assets, roots): lays a level out (expansion, isolateNodes, Clocks and resets) and draws it; request carries resolved ids and paths only ipSymbolImage.ts parseIpCoreDocument, renderIpSymbolImage(data, library, request, ...): the symbol of an .ip.yml with the caller's bus library imageEncoding.ts RenderLook, ImageEncoding, encodeImage: SVG text or PNG/JPG bytes renderResources.ts RenderAssets: fonts and bus libraries loaded once

The callers adapt it. The CLI (src/cli/render.ts) resolves names (--select, --expand) to ids, loads the built-in bus library and writes a file. The extension (src/providers/imageExport/ImageExportHost.ts) passes the graph the system viewer already shows (enriched by SystemDesignEnricher, unsaved edits included) and the IP core document text with the library the editor resolved, then asks where to save. The extension bundle loads ELK from dist/elk.bundled.js and the rasterizer from dist/resources/resvg.wasm, like the CLI.

Current view crops differ per editor. The system viewer sends the ids of the nodes inside its viewport (visibleNodeIds, from node positions and the React Flow transform); the service lays the level out with the Plex metrics and crops to the union of those nodes (cropNodeIds), because block sizes can differ from the canvas, which measures with the editor font. The IP symbol layout does not depend on font metrics, so the canvas viewport maps exactly to a layout rectangle (visibleLayoutRect) and the service crops to it (crop).

docs.title: Extension Host
docs.text: The extension host is the Node.js side of IPCraft. It can read files, register VS Code commands, start external tools, and create webviews. The webviews cannot perform these privileged tasks directly.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text: src/extension.ts is the entry point. During activation it registers providers, commands, views, and services with the extension context.

docs.title: Custom editors
docs.text:
Document Provider Webview *.mm.yml MemoryMapEditorProvider Memory Map editor *.ip.yml IpCoreEditorProvider IP Core editor recognized .tcl and .qsys system designs SystemDiagramProvider System diagram (read-only, opt-in)

A provider creates the webview, sends the current document, receives edits, and applies accepted changes through VS Code's document API.

SystemDiagramProvider registers ipcraft.systemDiagram with priority: option, so a system design opens in the text editor until the user asks for the diagram. It reads the document with readSystemDesign, enriches the graph, and posts it to the webview again on every document change or workspace trust grant. SystemDesignEnricher indexes workspace .ip.yml and HDL files and merges the pins of matching definitions into the graph. It reads nothing in an untrusted workspace. If enrichment takes longer than 100 ms, the provider posts the parsed graph first (with an info diagnostic) and the enriched graph when it is ready. The index excludes generated and dependency directories plus the search.exclude setting in the search itself (VS Code adds files.exclude), before the file limit applies.

The providers share these central services:

Service Plain-language role WebviewRouter Sends each incoming message to the matching handler DocumentManager Applies document writes in order and rejects edits based on old versions HtmlGenerator Creates secure webview HTML YamlValidator Checks documents against the IPCraft schemas ImportResolver Loads $import references in IP core files BusLibraryService Loads known interface definitions

docs.title: Document revisions
docs.text:
Each document update has a version. Each webview edit states which document version it was based on.

If the file changed after the webview's starting version, the host rejects the stale edit and sends the current document back. This prevents two updates from silently overwriting each other.

Asynchronous conformance and generation results also carry sourceRevision, which compares the exact source text before applying a result. This correlation guard is intentionally separate from the V-3/V-4 document revision protocol: it neither advances nor filters document versions. The full-text comparison is a deliberate per-result cost and should be considered if this mechanism is extended to larger or more frequent payloads.

See Data flow for the paired webview logic.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command modules under src/commands/ group the main workflows:

Area Examples Create Create IP core, memory map, or both Generate Generate RTL, tests, and vendor projects Import Read VHDL, Platform Designer, or IP-XACT files Build Run Vivado or Quartus and show reports Open external tools Open Vivado, IP Packager, Quartus, or Platform Designer Maintain Scan catalogs, migrate older files, switch editor mode

The complete user-facing list is in the commands reference.

docs.title: Generation and imports
docs.text:
src/generator/IpCoreScaffolder.ts coordinates code generation. It validates the source, prepares stable template data, renders the selected scaffold pack, and asks vendor toolchains for their output.

Importers under src/parser/ convert existing files into IPCraft documents:

  • VhdlParser.ts and VerilogParser.ts read HDL modules;
  • HwTclParser.ts reads Quartus component metadata;
  • ComponentXmlParser.ts reads Vivado IP-XACT component metadata;
  • VivadoInterfaceXmlParser.ts reads Vivado interface definitions for catalog discovery.

Import results still require user review because source formats do not always contain design intent.

docs.title: Vendor format boundary review
docs.text:
ComponentXmlParser, HwTclParser, and VivadoComponentXmlGenerator exceed the general module-size review threshold because each owns one ordered vendor format transformation: IP-XACT traversal, Tcl command traversal, or IP-XACT document assembly. Their syntax handling and source-order-dependent control flow remain local so the format can be read and reviewed in execution order. Format-independent policy and transformations are kept in focused shared modules, including contract property import and observed-port reconciliation.

The extraction rule is: logic with a second consumer belongs in src/shared/busContracts/ when it neither reads nor emits XML/Tcl syntax nor depends on vendor source ordering. This makes the size exception a cohesion decision, not an exemption from future extraction.

docs.title: Generator projection modules
docs.text:
registerProcessor.ts also exceeds the general module-size review threshold. It owns the one-way projection from normalized domain data into the template context: width-expression evaluation, register access derivation, bus-interface array expansion, and memory-map projection. These stages share the width and getString coercion helpers and run in a fixed order for every generated artifact, so they are reviewed together.

Policy that a second caller needs is extracted instead of grown in place:

  • resolvers/endiannessPolicy.ts decides which canonical ports need big-endian lane or bit reflow and how wide each reflowed element is. resolvers/bus.ts is the second consumer, so this policy must not live in registerProcessor.
  • resolvers/boundaryTransforms.ts plans the HDL-boundary signals that realize a reflow or a polarity inversion.
  • Contract-declared questions such as "is this a memory-mapped consumer" belong to src/shared/busContracts/, never to a generator-local name heuristic.

docs.title: External tools
docs.text:
Toolchains under src/services/toolchains/ provide one interface for local and Docker-based tools.

Commands ask the registry for a toolchain instead of reading installation settings themselves. BuildRunner streams output, and ReportParser extracts timing and size summaries for the Build view.

docs.title: Resource files
docs.text:
At activation, ResourceRoots locates templates, schemas, packs, and interface definitions inside the installed extension. Edit their source locations, not the copied files under dist/:

  • templates: src/generator/templates/;
  • packs: src/generator/packs/;
  • schemas and bus definitions: ipcraft-spec/.

docs.title: Generator Architecture
docs.text: The generator converts an .ip.yml file and linked memory maps into HDL, tests, and vendor project files. This page describes the contributor-facing design. Pack authors should start with scaffold packs.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text: src/generator/IpCoreScaffolder.ts coordinates the pipeline. It returns file contents to the staging workflow; it does not ask React components to write files directly.

docs.title: Main areas
docs.text: Area Location Responsibility Orchestration IpCoreScaffolder.ts Runs the complete generation flow Input preparation registerProcessor.ts Prepares maps, registers, and interfaces Template data contract/ and resolvers/ Defines and calculates values supplied to templates Bus rules buses/ Maps interface names to supported bus behavior Scaffold packs packs/ and ScaffoldPackLoader.ts Chooses output rules Rendering TemplateLoader.ts and templates/ Finds and renders Nunjucks templates Test generation testbench/ Combines a test framework with a simulator

docs.title: Stable template data
docs.text:
Templates receive a documented object rather than raw YAML. Its JSON Schema is src/generator/contract/template_context.schema.json. The generated TypeScript file templateContext.types.ts must not be edited by hand.

Before rendering, assertValidContext checks the object against the schema. A failure stops generation and reports the invalid values. In the source this check uses AJV, a JSON Schema validator.

Scaffold packs may declare apiVersion. IPCraft compares that range with the current template-data version before rendering:

Pack value Result Missing Accepted for older packs Compatible range such as ^1.0 Rendered normally Incompatible major version Rejected with a version error

docs.title: Resolvers
docs.text:
A resolver is a small conversion function that calculates one part of the template data.

Resolver Result Clock and reset Primary names, reset polarity, and clock periods Parameters HDL types, defaults, and Vivado UI groups Register behavior Software, hardware, write-one-to-clear, and change-event views Addressing Data width, byte width, and address width Bus Active bus signals, user ports, interrupts, and expanded arrays

Keep resolvers independent of file writing and template rendering. Their output is easier to test when it depends only on their inputs.

docs.title: Bus rules
docs.text:
BusRuleRegistry accepts full interface identities and short names, then returns one known bus rule. The rule supplies the short template name and whether the bus is memory mapped.

This keeps bus-name interpretation in one place. Templates should use normalized values such as axil or avmm instead of recognizing aliases themselves.

docs.title: Pack and template lookup
docs.text:
A workspace pack can replace a built-in template by using the same filename. Unchanged templates fall back to the built-in library.

Source templates live in src/generator/templates/ and are copied to dist/templates/ during compilation. Never edit the copied files.

docs.title: Width expressions
docs.text:
src/shared/evalWidthExpr.ts evaluates arithmetic width expressions for both the webview and generator. It supports numbers, parameter names, parentheses, and basic arithmetic without JavaScript eval.

Keeping one evaluator prevents the canvas preview and generated vendor metadata from calculating different widths.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Generator changes should prove progressively more:

Run the focused unit tests, then:

npm run generate-types   # only after schema changes
npm run compile
npm run test:integration:hdl

Run the matching EDA integration suite for vendor-specific changes.

docs.title: System overview
docs.text:
ipcraft-vscode is a VS Code extension with four webview surfaces:

Surface Files Kind IP Core editor *.ip.yml Visual editor Memory Map editor *.mm.yml Visual editor Data Inspector *.ipci.yml, or a panel opened from a register or port Analysis tool System diagram Vivado block design .tcl, Platform Designer .qsys and system .tcl Read-only viewer

The extension host is the Node.js process that can access VS Code and the file system. A webview is an embedded browser that renders one of these surfaces. They share domain types but communicate only through messages.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text: The extension host owns the VS Code document. The webview owns the visible editor state. Versioned messages keep them in step without losing external edits or re-applying the webview's own changes.

docs.title: Document open
docs.text:
1. VS Code calls resolveCustomTextEditor for a matching file.
  2. The provider creates the webview HTML and waits for a ready message.
  3. The provider sends update with the text and its docVersion. For IP core files it also sends the resolved imports.
  4. The webview parses the YAML with src/domain/parse.ts into the normalized model and adds editor-only values such as rowId.

docs.title: User edit
docs.text:
1. A component requests a path edit such as ['fields', 0, 'name'], or a structured operation such as ['__op', 'field-move'] so that no invalid intermediate state reaches the file.
  2. src/yamledit/ applies it to the parsed YAML document, keeping comments and number spellings such as hexadecimal values.
  3. Serialization removes rowId, __kind, and other editor-only values.
  4. The webview posts update with the full text, a monotonic editId, and the baseDocVersion it started from.
  5. WebviewRouter passes it to DocumentManager, which applies writes in order.

docs.title: Stale edits and echoes
docs.text:
If the document changed after baseDocVersion, the host rejects the edit and replies with forceResync: true. The webview drops:

  • an echo that carries its own completed edit ID;
  • an update older than the newest version it already shows.

src/services/WebviewRouter.ts and src/webview/sync/revisionFilter.ts implement the two sides of this rule. Change and test them together.

docs.title: Host commands
docs.text: The webview can post command (save, validate, openFile). The host runs the VS Code action and may show a notification.

docs.title: Canvas edit (IP Core only)
docs.text:
1. User drags an item from the library palette and drops it on the IpBlockCanvas
  2. useCanvasDrop resolves the payload into an IP Core update (e.g., push to clocks, ports, or busInterfaces)
  3. useCanvasUndo snapshots the prior YAML before applying the update
  4. updateIpCore writes the new value into the parsed model
  5. useIpCoreSync serialises the model back to YAML and posts type: 'update' to the host (same path as a form edit)

Canvas keyboard shortcuts (Delete, Ctrl+D, Ctrl+Z/Y) follow the same update path through updateIpCore.

docs.title: HDL generation
docs.text:
1. The user picks the HDL language, vendor targets, and scaffold pack in the IP Core toolbar and runs Scaffold Project or a generate command.
  2. The webview posts generate; IpCoreGenerateHandler runs IpCoreScaffolder, which renders every file in memory.
  3. The files are shown in the staging review (StagingPanel, WebviewStagingBridge). Nothing is written until the user confirms.
  4. The host posts generateResult with the written files or the error.

See Generator architecture.

docs.title: System viewer
docs.text:
A third, read-only surface shows Vivado write_bd_tcl scripts, Platform Designer .qsys systems, and Platform Designer system scripts as a diagram. It is not part of the YAML round trip: the files are read statically and never written.

Part Location Readers that turn a file into a vendor-neutral SystemGraph src/parser/system/ Detection and readSystemDesign entry point src/services/systemDiagram/ Custom editor provider (ipcraft.systemDiagram, priority: option) src/providers/SystemDiagramProvider.ts Workspace enrichment from .ip.yml and HDL files src/services/systemDiagram/SystemDesignEnricher.ts Webview (React Flow and elkjs layout) src/webview/systemDiagram/

docs.title: Build and Packaging
docs.text:
Output Location Extension bundle dist/extension.js Command-line bundle dist/cli.js Memory Map webview bundle dist/webview.js IP Core webview bundle dist/ipcore.js Data Inspector bundle dist/dataInspector.js System diagram bundle dist/systemDiagram.js Shared elkjs layout engine (system diagram page and CLI) dist/elk.bundled.js IBM Plex fonts for rendered images dist/resources/fonts/ Nunjucks templates and scaffold packs dist/templates/, dist/packs/ Compiled tests out/**

Built with webpack. See Development Setup for commands.

docs.title: Webview Security
docs.text: HtmlGenerator applies a Content Security Policy with default-src 'none'. Scripts, styles, fonts, and other resources are restricted to the extension's own webview.cspSource. Webviews cannot access the file system directly; all privileged operations cross the typed message bridge, and host commands are checked against an allow-list.

docs.title: YAML Libraries
docs.text: Library When to use js-yaml (v4) Read-only parsing or simple output where formatting does not matter yaml (v2) through src/yamledit/ Any edit written back to an existing document; keeps comments and hexadecimal spelling

docs.title: VSIX packaging contract
docs.text:
The production VSIX is an allowlisted runtime artifact. CI creates it once with npx vsce package, checks its archive contents, uploads that exact file, installs it into VS Code, and runs the extension-host smoke test against the installed copy.

The shipped content is limited to:

  • the extension manifest, VSIX metadata, README, changelog, MIT license, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md (the elkjs notice and EPL-2.0 text, and the IBM Plex notice and OFL-1.1 text);
  • the production extension and webview JavaScript/CSS bundles, third-party bundle license notices, and the bundled UI font;
  • every generator template and built-in scaffold pack copied from src/generator/;
  • dist/elk.bundled.js, the one copy of the elkjs layout engine: the system viewer page loads it with a script tag before systemDiagram.js (webpack external ELK) and dist/cli.js requires it (webpack external commonjs ./elk.bundled.js), so neither bundle embeds it and the VSIX does not pay for it twice (the file is copied unminified so its licence header stays);
  • the three IBM Plex WOFF (1.0) files (about 66 KB) under dist/resources/fonts/, which ipcraft render embeds in the SVG images it writes and, converted to TrueType in memory, hands to the rasterizer;
  • dist/resources/resvg.wasm, the unmodified resvg WebAssembly module that ipcraft render uses for PNG and JPG output (its JavaScript glue and jpeg-js are bundled into dist/cli.js);
  • the three runtime JSON schemas and every built-in bus definition copied from ipcraft-spec/;
  • the extension icon, concept resource, and walkthrough Markdown used by VS Code.

scripts/check-vsix.js rejects everything else, including source maps, node_modules, source and test files, fixtures, secrets, development configuration, and unreviewed new top-level content. It also requires every runtime source asset to be represented in the archive.

The size budget is 3.5 MiB compressed and 25 MiB unpacked. The budget was raised from 2 MiB and 5 MiB for elkjs, the layout engine used by the system diagram webview (issue #239; now the shared dist/elk.bundled.js), which brought the unpacked size to about 7 MB. The unpacked budget leaves headroom for further webview features. The compressed budget was raised again from 2.5 MiB to 3.5 MiB when the PNG and JPG rasterizer (resvg WebAssembly, about 2.4 MB, and jpeg-js) was shipped in the VSIX by decision, so ipcraft render --out x.png works everywhere (issue #268; VSIX 2168010 -> 3141774 bytes compressed, 7503857 -> 10033994 unpacked). The compressed budget still catches source maps or another development tree returning unnoticed. Any budget increase requires updating both this document and the constants in scripts/check-vsix.js with a reviewed reason.

docs.title: Marketplace release boundary
docs.text:
Marketplace release execution is a separate, manually dispatched GitHub Actions contract (.github/workflows/marketplace-release.yml): verify -> smoke -> protected publish -> postpublish. verify packages the versioned VSIX once, validates it, and uploads the immutable workflow artifact with its SHA-256 sidecar. Both smoke matrix legs download and checksum-verify that exact artifact before installing it on the minimum supported and stable VS Code versions. The protected vscode-marketplace GitHub environment downloads and verifies the same artifact before vsce publishes it through OIDC-federated Azure authentication (azure/login) — no Marketplace personal access token is stored anywhere. postpublish independently downloads the Marketplace package, validates its contents and metadata, then installs it for a stable smoke test.

The regular CI workflow deliberately does not publish: it validates changes on every push and pull request but does not own the Marketplace Contributor identity or the protected environment approval boundary. Only the manually dispatched Marketplace Release workflow can publish, so an identity-based OIDC credential, required environment reviewers, and a serialized concurrency group govern the only operation that can make a version public.

docs.title: Webview Architecture
docs.text:
IPCraft has two React applications running in VS Code webviews. A webview is an embedded browser: it can render the editor interface, but it cannot read project files or start external tools directly.

Editor Entry point Root element Memory Map src/webview/index.tsx #root IP Core src/webview/ipcore/IpCoreApp.tsx #ipcore-root

A third, read-only bundle, src/webview/systemDiagram/index.tsx, renders system designs (#system-diagram-root). It is described in System diagram application.

docs.title: Shared boundary
docs.text:
Both applications use src/domain/parse.ts to convert document data into the editor model and src/domain/serialize.ts to remove editor-only values before writing YAML.

rowId identifies a React row across renders. It is never document data.

docs.title: Memory Map application
docs.text:
The Memory Map app has three main regions:

  • Outline selects blocks, registers, arrays, and fields;
  • DetailsPanel chooses the editor for the selected item;
  • visualizers show bit and address layouts.

The table editors for blocks, registers, and fields share useTableEditorState. It combines keyboard navigation, draft protection, and the pointer insert bar.

Layout calculations belong in pure functions under src/webview/algorithms/. Components request an operation and render the result; they should not contain separate address or bit-position formulas.

docs.title: IP Core application
docs.text:
The IP Core app uses a block-diagram canvas:

  • LibraryPalette supplies items to add;
  • IpBlockCanvas draws ports, parameters, clocks, resets, and interfaces;
  • CanvasInspector edits the current selection;
  • StagingOverlay reviews generated files before they are accepted.

useIpCoreState owns parsed data and validation. useIpCoreBridge is the single typed message boundary: it sends serialized edits and applies the shared revision filter to incoming document updates. Canvas hooks handle drop, selection, undo, and keyboard actions.

Host conformance reports are sent as separate conformanceResult notifications tied to the exact source text they validate. They never bypass the document update filter, and the Issues session ignores a report whose source revision no longer matches the current YAML.

Generation is asynchronous, so generateResult carries the source revision captured when generation started. The Issues session discards a mismatched result before changing the report, opening the Issues panel, or focusing a canvas element. This correlation is separate from document-update revision filtering: a generation result is an operation response, not a document update.

docs.title: Bus contract package boundary
docs.text: src/shared/busContracts/index.ts is the public API used by generators, parsers, services, and the webview. Its exported modules cover canonicalization, normalization, resolution, validation, data-lane semantics, and vendor metadata import. Lower-level expression, constraint, fixpoint, alias, and active-port modules are implementation details; keeping them behind the barrel prevents consumers from coupling to intermediate resolver state.

docs.title: IP Core dependency and ownership boundaries
docs.text:
Keep the IP Core import direction one-way:

types and pure canvas utilities
  -> editor/message controllers and interaction hooks
  -> feature components
  -> IpBlockCanvas and IpCoreApp composition roots

IpCoreApp owns top-level composition and lifecycle. It must delegate document edits, revision-aware messaging, selection commands, session state, and overlay routing to typed boundaries rather than accumulating raw listeners, YAML path calculations, or feature state machines.

IpBlockCanvas owns canvas composition and rendering coordination. Geometry, selection transitions, drag and keyboard lifecycles, and model-changing commands belong in focused pure utilities, hooks, or controllers. Renderer callbacks request typed actions; they do not independently recreate mutations or cross-process messages.

Hooks may depend on neutral types and pure utilities, but not on React components. Move shared types or constants to a dependency-neutral module instead of importing them from a component. Cross-process messages must pass through the typed message boundary; do not add isolated postMessage calls or parallel message listeners inside feature components.

docs.title: Canvas inspector ownership
docs.text:
CanvasInspector.tsx owns only the resizable shell, header, footer, and feature router composition. Selection-specific panels, reusable inspector controls, message builders, and domain transformations live under components/canvas/inspector/. Panels receive explicit typed props rather than reading shared mutable module state.

Keep one inspector feature per production module. Aim for no more than roughly 400 lines; 500 lines is the review trigger for extracting controls, transformations, or a cohesive subfeature. A larger module should retain one clear responsibility and document why splitting it would make ownership less clear.

Apply the same size review to other production modules. Line count is evidence to inspect ownership, not a reason to split cohesive logic into arbitrary fragments. Generated files, declarative data, and templates are excluded.

docs.title: System diagram application
docs.text:
The systemDiagram bundle is read-only. It receives a SystemGraph from the host (graph, notRecognized, or error messages) and sends only ready, revealSource, openDefinition, the export and highlight messages, and startCompare, stopCompare and swapCompare.

While a comparison is on, the graph message also carries compare ({ baseLabel, currentLabel, canSwap, diff }, DiagramCompare in shared/messages/systemDiagram.ts; canSwap is true when the base is a file). The host owns the comparison; the webview only lists it. swapCompare asks the host to open the base file as a diagram and compare it with this document; the webview reaches it as onSwapCompare (useSystemDiagramMessages to BottomPanel). On the host, providers/systemDiagram/DiagramPanels.ts finds the panel of a document and holds a swap request until the new panel registers; PanelCompare.ts is the comparison of one panel (base, base file, start, stop, swap).

  • CompareControl.tsx is the toolbar control.
  • ChangesTable.tsx is the Changes tab, with one sticky bar (Base … → Current … by compareLabels.ts, Swap, the summary and the chips). It renders an address row as space → segment itself; ChangeRow and the Markdown report keep the one shared layout. Its rows are changeRows of the diff, with structured cells (CellPart, plain or code). changeTargets.ts resolves an address segment row to its slave block in the current graph. changeSummary.ts and panelFilter.ts hold the texts.
  • hooks/useBottomTab.ts decides when the tab opens and when it falls back.
  • The marks on the diagram (issue #302) follow the clock decoration pattern. changeMarks.ts is the pure model of a diff and the current graph: per block its status, title, marked pins and count of changes inside, per external port its status, per level the number of removed blocks and ports, and isNewWire, which decides from the gained peers of the diff whether a drawn wire is new (the labels come from peerLabel of the diff engine, so there is one spelling). changeDecor.ts computes from the layout and that model, once per layout and comparison, the NodeChange of each node, the ids of the new wires and the legend entries. useCanvasElements.ts merges them into the node data (change) and the edge data (changeNew); the per-node objects come from one memo, so a selection keeps them and useStableElements keeps the elements. NodeHeader draws the badges (ChangeBadges.tsx), the pins carry data-change and a title, and ElkEdge the new-wire stroke. The colors are the --sd-change-* custom properties at the top of systemDiagram.css, which the Changes tab uses too. hooks/useCompareView.ts owns the Marks toggle (on again when the base changes) and Changes only, which calls useIsolation's isolate with markedNodeIds; InstanceChanges.tsx is the Changes section of the Details (cells from ChangeCell.tsx, shared with the Changes tab). With Marks off the canvas gets no changes context and every one of these paths adds nothing.
Layer Owner Composition root SystemDiagramApp.tsx, DiagramWorkbench.tsx, WorkbenchLayout.tsx wire the toolbar, outline, canvas, details, and bottom panels Pure layout and geometry layout/ (elkjs graph construction, placementEdges.ts for which nets place the blocks, clockResetWires.ts, wireRoutes.ts and wireTree.ts (the tree of one net) for the clock and reset wires, node sizing, net badges, bounds, viewport policy, hover placement, panel sizes; expandedLayout.ts for hierarchy blocks expanded in place) and expansion.ts (which levels, nodes, and selections an expansion shows) Clock and reset analysis clocks/, pure and computed once per graph by analyzeClocks: clockTypes.ts (the result types), frequency.ts (parse and format), unionFind.ts and levelPaths.ts (small shared helpers), physicalNets.ts (nets joined across hierarchy pins, and the driver of each), clockRules.ts (declarative clock output, frequency, forwarding, generator, and reset rules; which Vivado IP pins are outputs is the shared src/domain/knownIpPins.ts, which the Vivado reader also uses to give those pins the direction out with source rule), clockDomains.ts, relatedClocks.ts (clocks of one generator), pinClocks.ts, resetSources.ts, crossings.ts, and the helpers each surface reads: crossingSummary.ts (counts and toolbar text), crossingEdges.ts, domainView.ts, treeSelection.ts, edgeView.ts, nodeView.ts (wire styles, pin marks, node strips), netTree.ts and treeChecks.ts (the tree rows and checks of Details), instanceClocks.ts, crossingRows.ts (the texts of its crossing rows), viewScope.ts (which domains, resets and crossings the Clocks and Resets tabs list for the level and expanded blocks on screen). clockDecor.ts merges them into one description of what the canvas adds to a layout Hooks hooks/ (host messages, ELK layout, per-level viewport, navigation with the expanded blocks, pin hover, panel resize; useSearchHistory.ts for the search box history, whose pure rules are in searchHistory.ts beside search.ts; searchMatcher.ts compiles the query and its options into the one matcher that the canvas dimming, minimap, counter, stepping and the outline result list share, and that the bottom panel's filter box reuses with the row texts of panelFilter.ts) Components the node, edge, panel, and table components in src/webview/systemDiagram/; FrameNode.tsx draws a hierarchy block expanded in place; ClocksTable.tsx and ResetsTable.tsx are the Clocks and Resets tabs, both listing crossings through CrossingsTable.tsx, ClockTreeDetails.tsx the clock and reset tree in Details, InstanceClockDetails.tsx the clocks of a block or port, AutoDetail.tsx and DiagramMinimap.tsx children of the React Flow canvas (the first sets the far-zoom detail, thresholds in layout/zoomDetail.ts; the second is the optional minimap, colored by minimap.ts), and DiagramToolbar.tsx groups its icon buttons with the shared ToolbarGroup and ToolbarSeparator (src/webview/shared/components/Toolbar.tsx)

messageState.ts keeps the last valid graph when a later message reports an error or says the file is no longer recognized, so the workbench and the user's view stay mounted. Layout and viewport decisions are pure functions that are tested without React.

A view's ELK layout depends on its level, its expanded blocks, and its isolation, and on no toggle. Its edges are the data and interface nets of the level, plus the clock and reset edges into a block that has no data edge, so that block stays next to its driver, and the first clock or reset edge of a driver that would otherwise have none, which only orders a clock or reset input port vertically next to one of its loads (placementEdges.ts). The boundary pins of the shown level form two columns by ELK layer constraints (layout/boundaryColumns.ts, used by boundaryNode): an input gets FIRST_SEPARATE and elk.alignment: LEFT, every other port (output, inout, unknown direction) gets LAST_SEPARATE and RIGHT, so the inputs share a left edge left of every block and the other ports share a right edge right of every block. ELK rejects a LAST_SEPARATE node with an outgoing edge to another LAST_SEPARATE node, so a right-column port that drives another right-column port (a net with no source endpoint) gets LAST instead, which ELK accepts before a LAST_SEPARATE target; it is placed in the last layer, which blocks can share. In a chain of such ports, where LAST to LAST would throw, the port that drives another driver stays unconstrained. The pins of clock and reset nets reserve a badge label, the net-name label at the end of their wire. ELK routes no clock or reset wire: after the layout toFlowElements calls clockResetWires (layout/clockResetWires.ts), which finds the terminals at the outer ends of the badges and routes one orthogonal tree per net and level with layout/wireRoutes.ts (pure geometry: block columns, channels, gaps, lanes), around the blocks. Lanes and crossings keep clear of the data wires; taps cross them. An expanded block's frame reserves room between its pin labels and its inner blocks (frameWireChannels in layout/expandedLayout.ts: a lane per inner clock or reset net ending on that side, at least FRAME_WIRE_CHANNEL), so the inner level has a channel for its trunks. They are ordinary flow edges (with a junction dot where a branch leaves the tree), listed before the data wires, so the viewer, the image export, and ipcraft render draw the same wires. A wire that branches off the tree also carries lead (the tree path from the driver to its first point), which the viewer draws with it: React Flow culls every edge by its own two nodes, so a trunk piece owned by an off-screen wire would otherwise vanish under the junction dots of wires that are on screen. The clock and reset wires are never dimmed. See Clock and reset wires. The Clocks and resets toggle only turns on the domain decorations of the clock context (which the unconnected-pin review pauses). Toggling therefore never runs ELK again, never moves a block, and never changes the viewport. isolationSubset picks its blocks the same way in every mode: the blocks within N data hops of the selected ones (hopDistances, a BFS over data and interface edges; N is 1 on every new isolation and is set from the toolbar stepper), with the edges of any category between two kept blocks at least one of which is closer than N, or all of them once N reaches the furthest hop (of which the layout draws the data wires and keeps the clock and reset edges that placementEdges selects). At N = 1 these are the selected blocks and the other end of each data wire.

Auto detail is not a layout input. AutoDetail.tsx (inside <ReactFlow>) sets data-far on the canvas container from a boolean store selector, so it re-renders only when the zoom crosses FAR_ZOOM (layout/zoomDetail.ts), and keeps --sd-name-scale in step through an imperative store subscription; systemDiagram.css hides pin text and scales block names under [data-far='true']. The scale is written only while far and in steps of NAME_SCALE_STEP (farNameScale), because changing an inherited custom property restyles every descendant of the canvas. The minimap is not a layout input either: DiagramMinimap.tsx only draws the nodes the canvas already holds, so toggling it never moves a block or changes the viewport.

Stable elements: hooks/useCanvasElements.ts (the node and edge building of DiagramCanvas.tsx) hands React Flow the previous node and edge object for every element that draws the same thing (reuseUnchanged in stableElements.ts, applied by hooks/useStableElements.ts), because React Flow skips an element whose object it already holds. A search keystroke or a selection therefore re-renders only the elements that changed. This holds only while everything put into a node's or edge's data is referentially stable for the elements it does not concern: callbacks are stable (onSelectNet reads the latest handlers from a ref), and per-node values (selectedNetIds, review, domains, pinMarks, highlightedPins) are computed in their own memos and set only on the nodes they apply to.

Dimming is not data: a dimmed block gets the node className sd-dimmed (the class of the React Flow wrapper, styled in systemDiagram.css), and reuseUnchanged keeps the previous data object when only the element around it changed. InstanceNode, FrameNode and BoundaryNode are React.memo, so such a block does not render its pins again.

<ReactFlow> sets onlyRenderVisibleElements, so blocks and wires off screen are not mounted. That only holds if every node carries measured (its layout size) and handles (the source and target handle of each pin, from layout/nodeHandles.ts), both set in toFlowElements. Without measured React Flow forgets the handle bounds of a node whose object changed and mounts the node again even off screen. With measured alone it would never read the handles again, so a renamed pin would keep its old handle id and lose its wire. Explicit handles make React Flow build the handle bounds from the layout every time, so an unmounted or unresized node never needs DOM measurement and its handle ids always come from the layout (React Flow may still re-measure a mounted node, which is harmless because the ids match); they must equal the <Handle>s the node components render (nodeHandles.test.tsx compares them). npm run perf:system-viewer measures these paths, including the mounted node count while zoomed in.

docs.title: Updates and drafts
docs.text:
Text cells keep an unfinished draft separately from the last valid document value. This allows users to type partial ranges or numbers without immediately creating invalid YAML.

When a valid edit is committed:

  1. the component requests an update;
  2. the domain model is serialized;
  3. the webview sends an edit ID and starting document version;
  4. the extension host applies or rejects the update;
  5. the webview accepts the resulting document version.

See Data flow for the message rules and bit field handling for structural field edits.

docs.title: Shared components
docs.text:
Reusable form and table controls are under src/webview/shared/components/. Shared validation, formatting, focus, and YAML-key helpers are under src/webview/shared/utils/.

Use VS Code theme variables for colors and keep form behavior consistent across both applications.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The extension host provides a content security policy that limits scripts, styles, fonts, and resources to approved extension locations. Webviews send typed messages for file access and commands. Do not add direct Node.js or file system assumptions to webview code.

docs.title: Contributor checklist
docs.text:
When changing a webview feature:

  • identify the owning layer and keep imports flowing toward the composition root;
  • extract a focused seam when a change would add another responsibility to a root or renderer;
  • keep dependencies explicit and avoid hidden module state or broad contexts;
  • use one tested implementation for behavior shared by multiple surfaces;
  • update both sides of a changed message;
  • keep editor-only fields out of serialized YAML;
  • use the shared table pattern in all parallel editors;
  • put layout calculations in pure algorithm modules;
  • preserve one gesture's update and undo boundary during refactors;
  • test focus and keyboard behavior in a browser;
  • verify narrow and wide editor widths;
  • verify light, dark, and high-contrast themes.

docs.title: Clock and Reset Wires
docs.text: The system viewer and the image export draw clock and reset nets as wires, routed over the data-flow placement by a small router of our own instead of ELK (issue #283).

docs.title: Why not ELK
docs.text:
Blocks are placed from data and interface nets only (issue #261, placementEdges.ts). ELK's layered layout puts every edge target in a later column than its source, so any clock or reset edge handed to ELK takes part in choosing the columns. Measured on the root levels of the fixtures, against the current placement:

Design Current (w x h, data wire px) All edges to ELK Second pass, edges oriented along the data columns zynq_dma_system 2521 x 577, 9566 2391 x 673, 13611 2959 x 703, 11131 versal_clocks 1417 x 528, 735 2233 x 405, 2071 2821 x 393, 2212 vivado_dsp_soc_8ch 4005 x 2657, 67220 4052 x 2869, 86643 4075 x 3763, 90815

ELK also draws one edge per sink, so a clock with 400 loads costs 400 routed edges. The router below keeps the placement untouched and costs a few percent of the ELK layout time.

docs.title: What is drawn
docs.text:
Element Rule Blocks and data wires Unchanged: placed and routed by ELK from data and interface nets. Clock and reset net One orthogonal tree per net and level, from the driver to every sink the level shows. Badge Stays, as the net-name label at each wire end. The wire starts just past the drawn text of the badge, so it never runs through it. Junction dot Where a branch leaves the tree. Two wires that cross without a dot are not connected. Expanded hierarchy block The inner level is routed inside the frame; its boundary pins are the frame pins. The frame keeps a wire channel between its pin labels and its inner blocks: 24 px (FRAME_WIRE_CHANNEL), or more when the clock and reset nets on that side need more lanes. Isolated view Only the clock and reset edges the isolation keeps are routed.

The viewer, Export image and ipcraft render share toFlowElements, so all three draw the same wires.

docs.title: Columns and channels
docs.text:
ELK's layered layout puts the blocks of a level in columns (its layers). The column of a block is found from the laid-out geometry: the x extents of the node bounds (nodeBounds, box plus badges) are merged where they overlap, and each merged interval is one column.

  • A channel is the free vertical strip between two columns, plus one before the first column and one after the last. A level with n columns has channels 0..n.
  • A gap is the free horizontal strip between two vertically adjacent blocks of a column, plus the open space above the first and below the last.

elk.separateConnectedComponents is off so that the columns hold for the whole level. With it on, ELK lays out each connected group of blocks on its own and packs the groups side by side, and their columns interleave (on versal_clocks the smallest channel was 11 px, on subsystem_two_clocks all blocks merged into one column). Turning it off costs no layout time and changes the size of those fixtures by under 2 percent.

docs.title: Routing one net
docs.text:
A terminal is the point where a wire meets a pin: the end of the drawn badge text, at the pin's height. It leaves towards the west or the east. A frame pin seen from the inner level has no badge on the inside. The strip where the frame draws its pin labels is an obstacle of the inner level, so no trunk or crossing runs through a label; the terminal is on the inner edge of the strip and leaves inwards, and the wire end is then extended to the frame border at the pin's height, below the label. The channel of a terminal is the first channel in the direction it leaves.

  1. Spine. Walking from the driver's channel outwards in both directions, as far as the outermost channel with a terminal, the net crosses each column through a gap. The crossing height is the free position nearest to the previous height (the driver's height at the start).
  2. Trunks. In every channel the net uses, one vertical trunk spans all its terminals and crossings there. Each terminal reaches the trunk by a horizontal tap at its own height. The tap is clear of blocks because a block's badges never overlap another block of its column.
  3. Lanes. Each net gets its own x position in a channel, 6 px apart and at least 4 px from the vertical segments of the data wires in that channel. The nets of a channel are in graph order, except that a net tapping from the left column is placed left of a net tapping from the right column at the same height, so two facing taps never run over each other. When a channel has fewer free positions than nets, the nets are spread evenly over it instead. Crossings in a gap are 6 px from each other and at least 4 px from the horizontal data wires that cross the column and from the heights of the terminals in the two channels beside it. A crossing also keeps 6 px from the crossings of the two neighbouring columns, which share a channel with it.

A pin that sits on two clock or reset nets is the terminal of both, so their taps share a line from the pin to the first trunk. This is the one case where wires of different nets overlap. 4. Wires. The tree is cut into one polyline per sink: sinks are taken nearest first, and each draws its path towards the driver until it meets a part an earlier sink drew. Every wire except the first of a net starts on the tree and gets the junction dot at its first point.

A wire is an ordinary flow edge (${net.id}#${endpointIndex}), so selection, highlight colors, the selected clock tree, dimming, and isolation treat it like a data wire.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Module Responsibility layout/wireRoutes.ts Pure geometry: columns, channels, gaps, lanes, and the spine and trunks of one net. Knows boxes, terminals, and polylines only. layout/wireTree.ts The tree of one net as points, and its cut into one polyline per sink. layout/clockResetWires.ts Builds the terminals and routing requests of each drawn level from the flow nodes and the graph, and turns the routes into flow edges. layout/elkLayout.ts toFlowElements adds the wires before the data wires, so data wires paint on top; separateConnectedComponents is off. ElkEdge.tsx, shared/render/systemLevelSvg.ts Draw the junction dot.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The router sorts the node boxes once per level. Per net it does work close to proportional to its terminals, plus a binary search over the gaps and occupied heights of each column it crosses. Measured results are recorded in issue #283.

docs.title: How the Data Inspector Decodes Values
docs.text: The Data Inspector decodes values from pasted literals, simulator waveforms, Vivado ILA, SignalTap, and CSV captures. It is an analysis tool and never edits an IP core, memory map, or generated HDL.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
The model separates four ideas:

  • a sample is temporary captured data;
  • a source has a stable name and width;
  • an operation derives one value from earlier values;
  • a field interprets a named bit range.

This separation lets a saved recipe work with new samples later.

docs.title: Four-state bits
docs.text:
src/dataInspector/BitVector.ts stores every bit as 0, 1, X, or Z. X means the value is unknown; Z means high impedance. Values from 1 to 4096 bits remain exact without relying on JavaScript's integer limit.

Ordering is fixed:

  • the highest bit appears on the left and bit 0 on the right;
  • the rightmost literal digit supplies the lowest bits;
  • concat(A, B) places A above B;
  • byte order and word order are independent capture settings;
  • extension and truncation require explicit operations.

Logical operations preserve useful known results. For example, unknown AND zero is zero, while unknown AND one remains unknown.

docs.title: Literals
docs.text:
parseLiteral.ts accepts sized Verilog values, VHDL binary and hexadecimal values, C-style 0b and 0x values, and decimal values with a width.

An input too wide for the selected width is rejected instead of silently truncated. Weak HDL states are normalized with a warning while the original text remains available.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Fields support hexadecimal, binary, unsigned, signed, enum, floating-point, and fixed-point views. Numeric results become unknown if required bits contain X or Z.

Fields in one overlay group cannot overlap. Different groups may describe alternative views of the same bits. Importing a register or port layout copies field metadata once; it does not create a live link to the memory map or IP core.

docs.title: Operation graph
docs.text:
Recipes store operations in dependency order. References between sources and operations become edges on the canvas.

Operation Width rule Concat Adds the two widths Slice Uses the selected inclusive range AND, OR, XOR, NOT Preserves width; binary operations require equal widths Shift Preserves width and inserts zeros Extend Increases to an explicit width Truncate Keeps low bits at a smaller width Byte swap Preserves a width divisible by eight

Connections that would create a cycle are rejected outright and the graph is unchanged. Every other connection is accepted, including one that joins incompatible widths. An operation becomes part of the recipe as soon as all its required inputs are wired, whether or not the result is valid.

A wired operation that breaks a width rule keeps its place on the canvas and shows the failing rule on the node. The recipe still counts it as a problem, so neither autosave nor manual save writes the file until the widths agree. This lets you correct a source width in place instead of rewiring the operation.

An operation with a missing input stays a draft. Drafts live only in the current webview and are never written to the recipe.

evaluateRecipe.ts evaluates the graph without side effects. Besides each result, it reports which source supplied every bit and which ranges were inserted, masked, or dropped.

docs.title: Capture import
docs.text:
vcd.ts indexes selected waveform signals and exposes values by timestamp. csvCapture.ts recognizes common Vivado ILA and SignalTap headers and imports one selected signal column at a time.

Captured samples remain temporary. Recipes save the decoding structure, not the potentially large capture content.

docs.title: Saved recipes
docs.text:
An .ipci.yml recipe stores source definitions, fields, operations, and useful view settings. It does not store pasted samples, VCD content, CSV rows, current selection, or panel sizes.

Canvas node positions may be stored so a shared recipe opens with a useful layout. Zoom and other temporary navigation state remain local to the session.

docs.title: Main implementation areas
docs.text:
Area Location Exact bit values src/dataInspector/BitVector.ts Literal parsing src/dataInspector/parseLiteral.ts Field validation and decoding src/dataInspector/fieldLayout.ts Graph edits src/dataInspector/recipeGraph.ts Evaluation src/dataInspector/evaluateRecipe.ts Capture readers src/dataInspector/vcd.ts, csvCapture.ts React interface Data Inspector webview components

For user instructions, see Using the Data Inspector.

docs.title: Documentation Screenshots
docs.text: IPCraft generates documentation screenshots from the compiled webviews. This keeps images aligned with the current interface and makes captures repeatable.

docs.title: Generate all screenshots
docs.text:
npm run docs:screenshots

The command builds the webview bundles, opens each documented state in Playwright, and writes light and dark PNG files to docs/images/.

Markdown pages embed only the light image because it also works well when the documentation is printed:

![Memory Map editor](../images/memorymap-editor-light.png)

Do not edit generated PNG files by hand.

docs.title: How capture works
docs.text:
The capture list is scripts/docs-screenshots/shots.ts. One entry describes the webview, input data, viewport, optional clipped element, and any interaction needed before capture.

export interface Shot {
  id: string;
  harness: 'memorymap' | 'ipcore' | 'dataInspector' | 'systemDiagram';
  source: string;
  viewport?: { width: number; height: number };
  clip?: string;
  scale?: 'css' | 'device';
  setup?: (page: Page) => Promise<void>;
}

The output name is docs/images/<id>-<theme>.png.

docs.title: Walkthrough frames
docs.text:
The landing page (docs/index.html) plays its walkthroughs as sequences of stills: anim-hierarchy-*, anim-unconnected-*, anim-isolate-*, anim-export-* and anim-inspect-*. Each frame is a shot whose setup repeats the steps of the frames before it, then draws a pointer where the user acts (showPointer). They use scale: 'css', one image pixel per CSS pixel, to keep the frames small. To regenerate only these, run npm run docs:screenshots -- -g anim-.

The export walkthrough also shows render-example-light.svg and render-example-dark.svg, written by ipcraft render from the same design:

node dist/cli.js render src/test/fixtures/system-design/zynq_dma_system.tcl \
  --out docs/images/render-example-light.svg --no-workspace
node dist/cli.js render src/test/fixtures/system-design/zynq_dma_system.tcl \
  --out docs/images/render-example-dark.svg --theme dark --no-workspace

docs.title: Add a screenshot
docs.text:
1. Choose a real example that clearly shows the feature.
  2. Add one entry to scripts/docs-screenshots/shots.ts.
  3. Use setup only when the capture needs a click, selection, or host message.
  4. Run npm run docs:screenshots.
  5. Inspect both theme variants.
  6. Add the light PNG to the relevant Markdown page.

Prefer one screenshot that explains a workflow over several images of similar states. Use a draw.io diagram instead when the page explains data flow, ownership, or internal architecture. Save it as an editable .drawio.svg in docs/images/diagrams/, in the light bahonavi palette of the diagrams already there, and embed it as an image.

docs.title: Supported webviews
docs.text:
Harness Content memorymap Memory Map editor ipcore IP Core editor dataInspector Data Inspector systemDiagram System diagram (design read by the real offline reader)

The harnesses live in src/test/browser/. They load the real compiled bundles without starting VS Code.

docs.title: Native VS Code views
docs.text:
The browser harness cannot capture views rendered by VS Code itself:

  • the IPCraft Build tree in the Explorer;
  • the template preview opened as a text editor;
  • native menus, notifications, and status-bar items.

Capture these manually in a clean VS Code window when a screenshot is essential. Use the light theme, crop to the relevant area, and avoid personal paths or unrelated extensions.

The Scaffold Pack Preview is a standalone webview. It could be automated with a dedicated harness, but it is not currently part of this pipeline.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
A normal browser does not provide VS Code color variables. The harness injects the matching variables before the webview starts so controls read the correct colors when they are created.

Theme files are under scripts/docs-screenshots/theme/. To refresh one from a running VS Code webview, open Developer Tools and copy its --vscode-* variables:

copy(
  ':root{' +
    Array.from(document.documentElement.style)
      .filter((name) => name.startsWith('--vscode-'))
      .map(
        (name) =>
          `${name}:${document.documentElement.style.getPropertyValue(name)}`,
      )
      .join(';') +
    '}',
);

Update the relevant CSS file and regenerate the screenshots.

docs.title: Important capture rules
docs.text:
• Wait for real content, not only the webview root element.
  • Fail when a required selector or state is missing.
  • Keep carets, hover effects, and transitions out of the result unless they are the subject of the image.
  • Use stable, representative project data.
  • Never include credentials, user paths, or private project names.
  • Keep Markdown image descriptions short and specific.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
After generating images:

  1. Confirm every expected light and dark file was updated.
  2. Confirm no image shows a loading state.
  3. Compare controls and text with the matching VS Code theme.
  4. Build the documentation:
python3 -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs build --strict
  1. Run npm run test:browser to confirm the shared browser harnesses still work.

Screenshot generation is intentionally not a required CI step. Run it when a UI change makes an existing image inaccurate or when a new visual workflow is documented.

docs.title: System viewer performance script
docs.text: A sibling developer tool measures how the system viewer responds on a large design. npm run perf:system-viewer builds the webview in production mode and runs scripts/perf/system-viewer.spec.ts (config config/playwright.perf.ts, never run by npm run test:browser or CI) on the harness above. It loads vivado_dsp_soc_64ch.tcl and vivado_dsp_soc_8ch.tcl and prints, for each action (search keystrokes, Enter, Escape, selecting a block, wheel zoom with Simplify zoomed out on and off, drag pan, Fit), the script, style and layout time from Chrome's Performance.getMetrics and the number and longest of the long tasks (over 50 ms). A JSON copy goes to test-results/perf/. Times vary by machine: compare runs on the same machine, before and after a change.

docs.title: How EDA Integration Tests Work
docs.text:
Unit tests can prove that IPCraft produced the expected text. They cannot prove that Quartus or Vivado accepts that text. EDA integration tests close that gap by running generated files through the real vendor tools.

EDA means electronic design automation. In this page it refers to Quartus and Vivado.

docs.title: What the tests prove
docs.text:
Each level answers a different question:

Check Question answered Unit test Did the generator choose the expected values? HDL compile Is the generated VHDL or SystemVerilog valid? Quartus validation Can Quartus read and use the generated project files? Vivado validation Can Vivado package and place the generated IP?

Passing a lower level does not guarantee that a vendor tool accepts the project. Vendor formats contain rules that a normal HDL compiler does not know.

For the exact feature-by-feature evidence and known gaps, see the generator feature coverage matrix.
