  2. Handle the drop/update in useCanvasDrop.ts (or the relevant use* hook under ipcore/hooks/)
  3. Render the element on IpBlockCanvas.tsx and add its property editor to CanvasInspector.tsx
  4. Update the IP Core Editor Reference

docs.title: Validation Flow
docs.text: cmake --build build --target validate runs lint, type check, unit tests, and compile in sequence and stops at the first error. The npm equivalent is in Testing.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Solution Custom editor does not appear Verify file extension and package.json custom editor selector. Check provider registration in src/extension.ts. Webview opens but no data Ensure webview posts { type: 'ready' }. Verify provider sends type: 'update'. Check useMemoryMapState. YAML updates not persisted Verify sendUpdate call path. Check WebviewRouter.useStandardDocumentHandlers's update handler and DocumentManager.updateDocument. Editor not updating Check webview console + extension host logs. Generator produces empty files Verify IP Core has a bus interface with memoryMapRef. Check template context in IpCoreScaffolder.buildTemplateContext. CMake configure fails (Node.js < 20) Install Node.js 20+ from nodejs.org. Docs targets unavailable Install Python 3, then re-run cmake -B build. Run cmake --build build --target docs_install first.

docs.title: Building a VSIX Package
docs.text: A VSIX file is an installable VS Code extension package. This guide builds one from the repository source.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Node.js 20+ and npm
  • All dependencies installed (npm install)

@vscode/vsce is already listed as a dev dependency — no global installation is required.

docs.title: 1. Install dependencies
docs.text: npm install

docs.title: 2. Run the production build
docs.text:
The package script compiles both the extension host and the webview bundles in production mode (minified, no source maps exposed):

npm run package

This runs webpack with --mode production --devtool hidden-source-map and outputs artefacts to dist/.

docs.title: 3. Package as VSIX
docs.text:
npx vsce package

This produces a file named ipcraft-vscode-<version>.vsix in the project root (e.g. ipcraft-vscode-0.8.6.vsix).

Tip

Steps 2 and 3 can be combined since vscode:prepublish automatically runs npm run package before vsce package: bash npx vsce package # triggers vscode:prepublish → npm run package first

docs.title: Installing the VSIX
docs.text:
Install directly in VS Code:

=== "VS Code UI" 1. Open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X / Cmd+Shift+X). 2. Click the ··· menu (top-right of the panel). 3. Choose Install from VSIX… and select the generated file.

Command line

bash code --install-extension ipcraft-vscode-0.8.6.vsix

docs.title: Verifying the package contents
docs.text:
Inspect what files are included without installing:

npx vsce ls

Files excluded by .vscodeignore (source files, node_modules, docs, src, etc.) will not appear in the output.

docs.title: Bumping the version
docs.text:
Use npm to update the extension version without creating a commit or tag:

npm version patch --no-git-tag-version   # or minor / major

This updates package.json and package-lock.json; retain the lockfile update. Then update packages/ipcraft/package.json to the same version and add the matching release heading to CHANGELOG.md (the user-facing release notes) and to docs/contributing/changelog.md (the developer changelog). The CLI packaging and release checks reject mismatched versions or a missing CHANGELOG.md heading.

Only after all five release files are ready, commit the complete release change and create its immutable tag:

git add package.json package-lock.json packages/ipcraft/package.json CHANGELOG.md \
  docs/contributing/changelog.md
git commit -m "chore(release): vX.Y.Z"
git tag vX.Y.Z
git push origin HEAD
git push origin vX.Y.Z

Do not move or replace the tag after a run has started.

Then re-run npx vsce package.

docs.title: Marketplace release runbook
docs.text: The production Marketplace release is operated from the Marketplace Release GitHub Actions workflow, not from a developer workstation. It is manually dispatched against an exact release tag and builds the VSIX once, uploads it as a versioned workflow artifact with a SHA-256 sidecar, smoke-tests that exact artifact on VS Code 1.80.0 and stable, and only then permits a protected publication.

docs.title: One-time Azure and Marketplace setup
docs.text:
Complete and periodically re-check the following configuration before attempting the first release:

  • Confirm the public Marketplace identity is bahonavi.ipcraft-vscode: publisher name bahonavi, publisher ID 68ba6820-f472-413e-8a4f-4be6765ede40, and extension ID 98c7d872-c2ba-4955-8ee5-5bf5e193ef78. In Marketplace management, manually confirm that the release administrators own this publisher and its extension before granting automation access.
  • In the GitHub repository, create an active tag ruleset targeting v*. Enable Restrict updates and Restrict deletions. Its bypass list must contain only explicitly designated, break-glass release administrators with Always allow; do not grant routine contributors, automation, or a broad administrator role a bypass. GitHub documents this as a New tag ruleset with a target pattern, protections, and a bypass list in its repository ruleset guide. This protection is a release prerequisite: do not create or run a release tag until it is active.
  • Create a user-assigned managed identity in Microsoft Entra ID, then add a federated credential on it scoped to a GitHub Actions issuer (https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com) with subject repo:bleviet/ipcraft-vscode:environment:vscode-marketplace. This lets the publish job authenticate to Azure with no stored secret — only workflow runs that pass the vscode-marketplace environment gate can mint a matching OIDC token.
  • Store the managed identity's AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, and AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID as environment secrets on the GitHub vscode-marketplace environment (Repository Settings → Environments), not as repository-wide secrets — this keeps them inaccessible to any job that doesn't target that environment.
  • Add that managed identity to the Marketplace publisher as a Contributor. The workflow uses vsce publish --azure-credential via azure/login's OIDC federation; it does not use a publisher personal access token (PAT).
  • Create the protected vscode-marketplace GitHub environment used by the publish job. Add required reviewers so a release needs explicit human approval before it can publish.
  • Do not store a Marketplace PAT in GitHub secrets, GitHub Actions variables, or anywhere else. The identity-based flow deliberately has no PAT secret to rotate or expose.

Microsoft documents secure automated Marketplace publishing, connecting GitHub Actions to Azure with OpenID Connect, GitHub's environment protection rules, and the VS Code extension manifest.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
1. Confirm the active v* tag ruleset described above blocks updates and deletions, with only the controlled break-glass administrator bypass. Then follow the version procedure above so the release commit includes matching extension and CLI manifests, the package-lock.json update, and the CHANGELOG.md heading before the immutable exact SemVer tag, vX.Y.Z (for example, v1.0.0), is created and pushed.
  2. Run the Marketplace Release workflow from the Actions tab (or gh workflow run marketplace-release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f publish=false), selecting that tag as the ref. publish: false is the default and performs no publication.
  3. Inspect the ipcraft-vscode-vsix workflow artifact: it must contain the versioned ipcraft-vscode-X.Y.Z.vsix and its .sha256 file. Review the verify job's checks and both smoke matrix legs, which install that artifact on VS Code 1.80.0 and stable after verifying its checksum.

docs.title: Publish
docs.text:
1. Re-run the workflow against the same tag protected by the active v* ruleset, with publish: true; do not create or package a different source revision between dry run and publication (gh workflow run marketplace-release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f publish=true).
  2. At the vscode-marketplace environment approval, review the versioned VSIX artifact and SHA-256 sidecar that the workflow checksum-verifies before the publish step. A required reviewer then approves the protected deployment.
  3. Wait for postpublish to finish. It polls the Marketplace for X.Y.Z, downloads the published VSIX, checks its Marketplace metadata and archive contents, and installs that downloaded package in a stable VS Code smoke test.
  4. Perform the Marketplace listing review below. Only after the extension has published and been verified may the operator run the existing Publish CLI to npm GitHub Actions workflow for the matching version.

docs.title: Marketplace listing review
docs.text:
The pipeline validates the archive and Marketplace API metadata, including the required README, license, changelog, icon file, identity, links, categories, and contributed commands. It cannot judge presentation. A release administrator must open the public listing and manually review:

  • rendered icon and README;
  • homepage, repository, and issue links;
  • categories and visible commands;
  • license and changelog or release notes; and
  • installation from the Marketplace in VS Code.

This human visual check is distinct from the automated archive/API checks and the post-publication installation smoke test.

docs.title: Failure and recovery policy
docs.text:
• A failure before publication is safe to rerun after correcting the cause. Keep the same tag only while it still represents the intended, immutable release source.
  • Never reuse an existing Marketplace version or silently skip a version. The release contract rejects a version that is already listed.
  • If publication may have succeeded but postpublish fails, retain the workflow artifact, its SHA-256 sidecar, and diagnostics. Diagnose the published listing and downloaded VSIX against that retained evidence before taking another action.
  • Prefer a corrected, higher version for a replacement release.
  • Use Unpublish only when the published extension must be withdrawn. Do not use Remove or version deletion as routine rollback: those actions are irreversible and removed version numbers cannot be reused.

docs.title: Releasing the standalone CLI
docs.text:
The VSIX and the npm CLI are separate artifacts. The VSIX bundles ipcraft and puts it on PATH in VS Code terminals (see Command line); the npm package is for machines without VS Code.

Build and test the npm archive locally without publishing it:

npm run package:cli
npm run test:cli-package

After the matching extension version has been published and verified through the Marketplace release runbook, run the Publish CLI to npm GitHub Actions workflow manually. Enter the matching version and confirm that the extension is already published. The workflow checks the versions, rebuilds the production bundle, installs the tarball in a clean temporary project, and only then runs npm publish. The protected npm environment must provide NPM_TOKEN.

Direct publication is locked unless IPCRAFT_PUBLISH=confirmed is supplied, so normal builds, tests, and npm pack cannot publish the package.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Solution ERROR Missing publisher name Ensure publisher is set in package.json (currently bahonavi). ERROR It seems the README.md still contains template text Update README.md to remove placeholder content. Build fails before packaging Run npm run package separately first and resolve any webpack errors. VSIX installs but extension does not activate Check dist/extension.js exists. Ensure "main": "./dist/extension.js" in package.json.

docs.title: Building a Project
docs.text: IPCraft can run Vivado or Quartus without opening the vendor interface. This is called a headless build. Tool output, timing, and resource use appear in VS Code.

docs.title: Before you build
docs.text:
You need:

  • an .ip.yml file;
  • generated Vivado or Quartus project files;
  • the matching tool configured locally or through Docker.

Run IPCraft: Scaffold Project (RTL + EDA packaging + Testbench), Generate Vivado Project, or Generate Quartus Project first if no build target exists.

docs.title: Run the build
docs.text:
1. Open the IP core.
  2. Run IPCraft: Build.
  3. If prompted, choose a target.
  4. Follow live messages in the IPCraft Build output channel.
  5. Review the Build panel in the Explorer when the tool finishes.

docs.title: Choose a target
docs.text:
Target Work performed Best use Vivado out-of-context synthesis Synthesizes the IP core alone Fast syntax, clock, and resource check Vivado full implementation Synthesizes, places, and routes Final timing for the chosen part Quartus compile Synthesizes, fits, and analyzes timing Complete Quartus result

Out-of-context means the IP core is built by itself, outside a complete FPGA system. XPR is Vivado's saved project format.

docs.title: Read the result
docs.text:
The Build panel reports:

  • pass, fail, or running state;
  • timing summary;
  • resource use such as lookup tables, registers, memory blocks, and DSP blocks;
  • links to the complete vendor reports.

Timing slack is the margin between the required and actual signal arrival time. A negative worst slack means at least one path misses its timing requirement.

Vivado — OOC           PASS
├── Timing
│   ├── Worst setup slack: +1.234 ns
│   └── Failing paths: 0
└── Resources
    ├── LUT: 1,234 / 53,200
    ├── FF:  2,891 / 106,400
    └── BRAM: 4 / 140

Select a report node to open the underlying file.

The panel is native VS Code interface, so it is not part of the automated webview screenshot pipeline. See documentation screenshots for the capture boundary.

docs.title: Report locations
docs.text: Target Directory Vivado out-of-context xilinx/build/ooc/ Vivado full implementation xilinx/build/xpr/ Quartus compile altera/build/output_files/

docs.title: Status bar
docs.text: The IPCraft status item shows whether a build is running, passed, or failed. A successful Vivado build shows worst timing slack; a successful Quartus build shows maximum clock frequency. Select the item to reopen the output channel.

docs.title: Configure a local tool
docs.text:
List every installed version. IPCraft detects the version of each folder and, for an existing project, uses the version the project was created with:

{
  "ipcraft.vivado.runner": "local",
  "ipcraft.vivado.installDirs": ["/tools/Xilinx/Vivado/2024.2", "/tools/Xilinx/Vivado/2025.1"],
  "ipcraft.quartus.runner": "local",
  "ipcraft.quartus.installDirs": ["/opt/intelFPGA_pro/23.1"],
  "ipcraft.build.jobs": 4
}

Leave the list empty when the tool command is already on PATH. To always use one version in a workspace, set ipcraft.vivado.pinnedVersion or ipcraft.quartus.pinnedVersion. With an .xpr or .qpf project file open, IPCraft: Select Vivado Version or IPCraft: Select Quartus Version picks and pins the version for you.

docs.title: Configure Docker
docs.text:
Give each image a version label, because an image reference cannot be parsed into a version:

{
  "ipcraft.vivado.runner": "docker",
  "ipcraft.vivado.dockerImages": [{ "label": "2024.2", "image": "cvsoc/vivado:2024.2" }]
}

Quartus uses the equivalent ipcraft.quartus.runner and ipcraft.quartus.dockerImages settings.

The single-folder settings ipcraft.vivado.installDir, ipcraft.vivado.dockerImage, ipcraft.quartus.installDir, and ipcraft.quartus.dockerImage are deprecated; use the lists above.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Problem Check No build targets Generate the vendor project first Tool not found Installation directory, PATH, or Docker image Build command fails First vendor error in the IPCraft Build output channel Panel has no report Confirm the vendor wrote files to the expected directory Negative timing slack Clock constraints and the critical path in the timing report

For raw commands and every setting, see the commands and settings reference.

docs.title: Checking Consistency
docs.text:
Consistency checking finds drift: a difference between the IP core description and the HDL or vendor files that are meant to match it.

Generated files can be hand-edited after scaffolding — a signal renamed in the top-level entity, a port added directly to the HDL, a component.xml regenerated by Vivado. Consistency checking cross-references the .ip.yml spec against those artifacts and reports every mismatch in both directions, so drift is caught before it causes an integration failure.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • An IP Core (.ip.yml) that has already been scaffolded at least once, so a top-level HDL file exists to check against

docs.title: Choose a check
docs.text:
Command Compares the spec against Use when IPCraft: Check Consistency The top-level HDL entity/module for every file in fileSets, plus altera/<name>_hw.tcl and xilinx/component.xml if they exist You want the full picture, including generator-owned files that would be silently overwritten on the next generate IPCraft: Check HDL Consistency (managed:false) Only HDL files explicitly marked managed: false (hand-authored, never touched by generation) You only care about drift in files you deliberately protected from regeneration

Both are available from the Command Palette, the .ip.yml editor title bar, the Explorer/editor context menu, and the IPCraft menu.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
1. Open the .ip.yml file (visual editor or text editor)
  2. Run IPCraft: Check Consistency (or the HDL-only variant) from the Command Palette
  3. A toolbar badge in the visual editor also runs the full check automatically whenever the editor opens and whenever the HDL or vendor files it depends on change, so you may already see a result before running the command manually

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
Results appear in three places at once:

Location What you see Toolbar badge (visual editor) A live count reflecting the current state — click it to open the findings panel Findings overlay panel Every finding, grouped by source, with Re-check and Keep .ip.yml & Regenerate actions Output channel (IPCraft Consistency Check / IPCraft HDL Consistency) The same findings as plain text, plus an information/warning toast

Each finding has a kind — missing-port, extra-port, direction-mismatch, width-mismatch, parameter-default-mismatch, missing-register, field-range-mismatch, and others — and a severity:

Severity Meaning Amber A difference that can usually be added safely, such as a new HDL port not yet in the specification Red A conflict that needs a decision, such as a missing port or different width

There is no diff view opened directly by this feature — pair it with the diff shown in the staging overlay when you re-scaffold to see the actual text change.

Interface drift of existing HDL files (ports or generics that differ from the newly generated entity or module) is also shown as a badge during staging; see Review staged files.

docs.title: Resolving findings
docs.text:
Finding kind Typical fix Extra port/parameter in HDL Add the matching field to the .ip.yml spec (canvas or YAML), or ignore the finding if the addition was intentional and out of scope for the spec Missing port/parameter in HDL Someone deleted it by hand — either restore it in the HDL or remove it from the spec Direction/width/default mismatch Decide which side is correct, then edit the other to match Missing register/field-range mismatch Regenerate the register file, or reconcile the memory map manually if the HDL was hand-tuned

After fixing the spec side, re-run IPCraft: Scaffold Project (RTL + EDA packaging + Testbench) (see Generating a Project) to bring the generated files back in sync, or edit the HDL directly if it is managed: false.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Generating a Project — regenerate files once the spec is corrected
  • Building a Project — run a headless synthesis build once the spec and HDL agree

docs.title: Creating Your First IP Core
docs.text: How to go from an empty folder to a generated RTL project using the visual canvas editor.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• IPCraft installed in VS Code
  • An empty workspace folder (or any folder you want to add the IP core to)

docs.title: Create the file
docs.text:
1. Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P)
  2. Run IPCraft: New IP Core (use IPCraft: New IP Core + Register Map instead if your core needs memory-mapped registers — see Memory-Mapped Registers)
  3. Choose a file name — this becomes the core's default name in the spec

IPCraft creates <name>.ip.yml and opens it in the visual canvas editor. The file is the single source of truth for the core — its VLNV, clocks, resets, ports, bus interfaces, and code generation settings all live here as plain, version-controllable YAML:

vlnv:
  vendor: user # from the ipcraft.import.vendor setting
  library: my_library
  name: my_core # taken from the file name you chose
  version: 1.0.0
description: A new IP Core definition

VLNV means vendor, library, name, and version. Together they identify the core across files and tools. Set ipcraft.import.vendor once if you want new cores to use your organization by default.

You can switch to the raw YAML at any time with Ctrl+Shift+V.

docs.title: The canvas
docs.text:
The canvas renders the core as a live block diagram. Every change made in the Library Palette or Inspector is reflected here instantly, and vice versa.

Panel Location Purpose Library Palette Left Draggable primitives: generics, infrastructure (clocks/resets/ports/interrupts), bus protocols IP Block Canvas Center The SVG schematic — clocks/resets on the left edge, ports and bus interfaces on the right, generics along the bottom Inspector Right Properties of whatever is currently selected on the canvas Key Action Delete Remove the selected element Ctrl+D / Cmd+D Duplicate the selected element Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y Undo / Redo Ctrl+0 / Cmd+0 Reset zoom to 100% Ctrl+Wheel Zoom in / out Plain wheel / middle-mouse drag / Space+drag Pan Ctrl+F / Cmd+F Open port search

See the IP Core Editor Reference for the full component and validation model.

docs.title: Add clocks, resets, and ports
docs.text:
Drag each element from the Library Palette's Infrastructure category onto the canvas — clocks and resets go on the left edge, ports on the right edge. Click any placed element to edit its fields in the Inspector.

Element Key fields Clock Name (e.g. clk, axi_clk); optional frequency hint used for timing-aware vendor packaging; associated reset Reset Polarity — activeLow (default, rst_n) or activeHigh (rst); associated clock Port Name, direction (in / out / inout), width (numeric or a generic reference) Generic/Parameter Integer, boolean, or string variant — exposes a VHDL generic / SystemVerilog parameter at integration time

The canvas colors each clock domain differently, so with two clocks every port associated with clk_a appears in one color and clk_b ports in another — clock-domain crossings become visible at a glance.

docs.title: Add a bus interface
docs.text:
A bus interface groups related signals (address, data, handshake) into one named connector. IPCraft knows the signal maps for common bus standards, so you describe what the interface is rather than wiring every signal by hand.

  1. Open the Library Palette — bus types are grouped under Protocols
  2. Find the bus type you need (e.g. AXI4-Lite Slave), or use the search box to filter
  3. Drag it onto the right edge of the canvas block
  4. Click the new bus interface, then edit its fields in the Inspector
You want… Use Register access (control/status) AXI4-Lite Slave or Avalon-MM Slave Burst DMA from the core AXI4 Master Simple memory-mapped I/O APB Slave Custom/proprietary bus Custom Interface (conduit) — see Custom interfaces

The Inspector's physicalPrefix field sets the HDL signal prefix, e.g. s_axi_ → s_axi_awaddr, s_axi_awvalid.

docs.title: Generate your RTL
docs.text:
Run IPCraft: Scaffold Project (RTL + EDA packaging + Testbench) from the Command Palette, the editor title bar, or the IPCraft menu. It generates RTL, a testbench, and vendor project files in one step — see Generating a Project for the full output layout and per-piece generation commands.

Output What it is <name>.vhd / .sv Top-level entity/module instantiating core + bus wrapper <name>_core.vhd / .sv User logic skeleton — this is where your code goes <name>_pkg.vhd / .sv Register constants and types package <name>_axil.vhd / <name>_avmm.vhd (+ .sv) Bus wrapper matching the bus type on your register-mapped slave interface <name>_regs.vhd / .sv Register decode logic (if a register map is linked) tb/<name>_test.py, tb/Makefile cocotb test skeleton and simulation Makefile component.xml / <name>_hw.tcl Vivado IP-XACT / Platform Designer component (per configured target)

docs.title: Review and accept the staged output
docs.text:
Before anything is written to disk, IPCraft shows a staging overlay with exactly what will happen:

Status Meaning New File does not exist yet — will be created Modified Existing file whose content differs — will be overwritten unless excluded Unchanged Generated content is identical to what's on disk — no write needed Protected (lock icon) User-owned file (managed: false) — excluded from Apply by default

Click View Diff next to any modified file to open a side-by-side diff before committing. Click Confirm & Apply to write all staged, non-excluded files, or Cancel to discard the run.

A file is only protected from overwrite if something explicitly marks it managed: false — either a fileSets entry you add yourself, or a scaffold pack rule. The default builtin-ipcraft pack does not mark <name>_core.vhd as protected, so re-running Scaffold Project regenerates it from the template and any hand-edited logic there is overwritten unless you protect it explicitly.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Generating a Project — every generation command and the full output layout
  • Building a Project — run a headless Vivado/Quartus build against the generated files
  • Memory-Mapped Registers — link a register map to a bus interface
  • Prefer to follow along inside VS Code? Run IPCraft: Open Walkthrough... → Design Your First IP Core

docs.title: Customizing Generated Files with Scaffold Packs
docs.text:
A scaffold pack controls which files IPCraft generates and where it puts them. Use one when the built-in file layout does not match your project.

A pack contains:

  • scaffold.yml, which lists the output files;
  • optional .j2 templates, which describe their contents.

.j2 files use Nunjucks, a template language that replaces names such as {{ name }} with values from the current IP core.

docs.title: Choose a pack
docs.text:
IPCraft includes these packs:

Pack Use it when builtin-minimal You need one empty top-level HDL file builtin-ipcraft You want the complete IPCraft RTL structure example-register-only Your project already has most RTL and needs only register decoding example-no-regfile You want IPCraft's structure but will write the register decoder yourself example-with-docs You also want generated Markdown register documentation

Open an .ip.yml file and select a pack from Scaffold Template in the editor toolbar.

The selection is saved with the IP core. If the file does not choose a pack, IPCraft uses the workspace setting ipcraft.generate.scaffoldPack, followed by builtin-minimal.

docs.title: Preview a template
docs.text:
1. Open a .j2 file.
  2. Run IPCraft: Preview Template Output from the Command Palette or editor title bar.
  3. Choose an .ip.yml file if the workspace contains more than one.
  4. Save the template to refresh the preview.

The preview is read-only. Use IPCraft: Pin Preview IP Core to change which IP core supplies the preview data.

docs.title: Create a pack from a built-in pack
docs.text:
This is the simplest way to begin:

  1. Run IPCraft: Export Built-in Scaffold Pack.
  2. Select the closest built-in or example pack.
  3. Enter a short folder name, such as aurora-rtl.
  4. Open the exported scaffold.yml.

IPCraft writes the copy under:

.vscode/ipcraft/packs/aurora-rtl/
├── scaffold.yml
├── top.vhdl.j2
├── top.sv.j2
└── ...

The Scaffold Pack Preview beside scaffold.yml shows the resulting file tree:

rtl/
├── spi_controller_pkg.vhd       generated
├── spi_controller.vhd           generated
├── spi_controller_core.vhd      protected
└── spi_controller_regs.sv       skipped: condition is false
  • generated means IPCraft will write or replace the file;
  • protected means IPCraft writes it once and then leaves it alone;
  • skipped means the file's condition does not match the current IP core.

docs.title: Create a small pack from scratch
docs.text:
Create this directory:

.vscode/ipcraft/packs/my-pack/
├── scaffold.yml
├── top.vhdl.j2
└── top.sv.j2

Add a manifest:

.vscode/ipcraft/packs/my-pack/scaffold.yml
name: "my-pack"
description: "One top-level HDL file"
fullGeneration: false

files:
  - source: "top.vhdl.j2"
    target: "rtl/{{ name }}.vhd"
    condition: "not is_systemverilog"

  - source: "top.sv.j2"
    target: "rtl/{{ name }}.sv"
    condition: "is_systemverilog"

Then select my-pack from Scaffold Template and generate the project.

docs.title: Manifest fields
docs.text:
Field Required Meaning name Yes Pack name shown by IPCraft description No Short explanation shown in the preview fullGeneration No Gives generated tests the complete register and bus data when true. A full-generation pack that declares testbench-like output and its own build/run entry point owns the complete output tree, so IPCraft does not append framework, docs/, altera/, or xilinx/ files generateFrameworkTestbench No Explicitly enables or suppresses IPCraft's tb/* and .vscode/settings.json framework testbench output. When omitted, it remains enabled for compatibility unless the pack owns the complete output tree requirements No Input compatibility this pack needs — see below generation No Generation defaults this pack prefers — currently indentation — see below files Yes Output rules files[].source Yes Template to render files[].target Yes Output path, relative to the generated project files[].condition No Generate only when the expression is true files[].managed No Replace on later runs unless set to false files[].executable No Set the POSIX executable bit after writing the file

Use managed: false for files that users are expected to edit. IPCraft creates the file on the first run and does not replace an existing copy later.

- source: "core.vhdl.j2"
  target: "rtl/{{ name }}_core.vhd"
  managed: false

Use executable: true for pack-owned helper scripts that must be runnable directly (./script.sh) instead of only via bash script.sh. IPCraft sets the owner/group/other execute bits after writing the file, without touching any other permission bit already present. This has no effect on filesystems that don't support POSIX permission bits (e.g. some Windows/exFAT mounts) — ipcraft verify compares file content only and never reports a mode-only difference as stale.

- source: "qsys_tb_gen_sh.j2"
  target: "qsys/qsys_{{ name }}_tb_gen.sh"
  executable: true

docs.title: Declare input requirements
docs.text:
A pack that only makes sense for certain IP cores can declare requirements in scaffold.yml. IPCraft checks these before rendering any file — an incompatible IP core fails generation with a clear reason instead of producing a partial or invalid file tree.

requirements:
  hdlLanguages:
    - vhdl
  busTypes:
    - avmm
  memoryMappedSlave: required
  logicalPorts:
    - address
    - read
    - write
    - writedata
    - readdata
Field Meaning hdlLanguages HDL languages this pack supports (vhdl, systemverilog) busTypes Bus type ids this pack supports (axil, axi4, avmm, axis, avst) memoryMappedSlave required or forbidden — whether the IP core must (not) have a memory-mapped slave interface logicalPorts Logical port names (case-insensitive) that must be active on the primary bus interface — useful for buses such as Avalon-MM where every port is optional, so an interface with no enabled ports would otherwise render with no signals

Omitting requirements entirely (or any field within it) imposes no constraint on that dimension — existing manifests keep working unchanged.

docs.title: Declare an indentation default
docs.text:
A pack can declare its own preferred indentation for generated HDL and synthesis-tool source files, so a workspace with several packs for different consumers (for example, an internal RTL pack that wants four spaces and a vendor-delivery pack that wants tabs) doesn't need the user to change workspace settings or remember pack-specific CLI flags between runs.

generation:
  indentation:
    style: tab

generation:
  indentation:
    style: spaces
    size: 4
Field Meaning style spaces or tab size Spaces per indentation level. Ignored when style is tab

Indentation is resolved independently per field, in this precedence order:

  1. An explicit CLI flag or programmatic run option (--indent-style, --indent-size, or the equivalent explicit GenerateOptions value)
  2. The selected scaffold pack's generation.indentation value
  3. VS Code workspace/user defaults (ipcraft.generate.indentStyle and ipcraft.generate.indentSize)
  4. The built-in fallback (spaces, size 2) when no VS Code configuration is available, such as headless library use

A pack may set only style, only size, or both — an omitted field falls through to the next tier. An invalid style or size fails pack loading with an error naming the pack and the offending field; omitting generation or generation.indentation imposes no pack-level default, so existing manifests are unaffected. ipcraft generate and ipcraft verify resolve indentation identically for the same pack and flags.

docs.title: How templates are found
docs.text:
IPCraft checks the selected pack first and then the built-in template library. You only need to copy templates you want to change.

The same rule applies to Cocotb and vendor project templates. A custom component.xml.j2 is different: it replaces the complete Vivado component file, not part of it.

docs.title: Template values and conditions
docs.text:
Templates and condition expressions receive the template data described in the generator reference, for example name, is_systemverilog, has_memory_mapped_slave, bus_type, and registers.

Common conditions are:

condition: "not is_systemverilog"
condition: "is_systemverilog"
condition: "has_memory_mapped_slave"
condition: "includeRegs and has_memory_mapped_slave"

docs.title: Verify the pack
docs.text:
Before sharing a pack:

  1. Preview every changed template.
  2. Check generated and skipped files in the file-tree preview.
  3. Generate both supported HDL languages when applicable.
  4. Compile the generated HDL.
  5. Run the generated tests.

For a complete example, follow Build and verify your own scaffold pack.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Check Pack not found Folder name and .vscode/ipcraft/packs/<name>/scaffold.yml Template not found The resolved source name in the pack or built-in library File always skipped Its condition in the Scaffold Pack Preview Preview has no IP core Create an .ip.yml file or pin an existing one Preview does not refresh Save the .j2 file Protected file is replaced Confirm the rule has managed: false and the file already exists

docs.title: Custom Interfaces
docs.text:
A custom interface is a named group of signals that does not follow one of IPCraft's built-in protocols, such as a proprietary streaming link or a diagnostic port. A conduit is such a group with no implied bus transaction.

Use a built-in interface (AXI, Avalon) or one from the Vivado interface catalog when one matches: vendor tools then understand the interface and can connect it automatically. Use a custom interface for everything else.

Interface Signal list Tool understanding AXI or Avalon Fixed by the protocol Vivado or Quartus understands the bus Vivado catalog Supplied by Vivado Vivado understands the interface identity Custom Defined by you Tools keep the group but may not connect it automatically

docs.title: Add the interface
docs.text:
1. In an .ip.yml open in the IP Core editor, find Custom Interface under Bus Protocols in the library on the left.
  2. Drag it onto the edge of the core block.
  3. Select the new interface; the inspector opens on the right.

docs.title: Configure it
docs.text:
In the inspector's Configuration section:

Field What it controls Mode conduit for a signal group without transactions; master or slave when one side clearly initiates Physical Prefix HDL signal prefix, for example dbg_ gives dbg_trace_data Interface Type Empty for a one-off conduit, or vendor, library, name, and version for a reusable identity

slave and conduit interfaces are drawn on the left of the block, master interfaces on the right.

docs.title: Add signals
docs.text:
In the Signals section, select Add signal for each wire:

Field Meaning Direction in, out, or inout, seen from this interface's mode; the opposite mode sees the reverse Name Appears in the RTL port list as <physicalPrefix><name> Width A number or a parameter name; empty for one bit Presence REQ (always generated) or OPT (generated only when the core enables it); click the badge to toggle

The signals are stored inline in the .ip.yml:

busInterfaces:
  - name: DIAG_OUT
    type: ipcraft:busif:conduit:1.0
    mode: conduit
    physicalPrefix: diag_
    conduitPorts:
      - name: ENABLE
        direction: in
      - name: SAMPLE
        direction: out
        width: 12
      - name: STATUS
        direction: out
        width: 3

docs.title: Reuse across IP cores
docs.text:
An inline interface belongs to one core. To share the same signals between cores:

  1. Select the interface and select Save Bus Definition in the inspector.
  2. Choose a name. IPCraft writes <name>.busdef.yml and switches the interface to reference it.
  3. In another core, add a Custom Interface and pick the saved definition.

Files named *.busdef.yml anywhere in the workspace are discovered automatically and offered as interface types. A core can also point to a folder of definitions with useBusLibrary. Editing a .busdef.yml updates every core that uses it.

docs.title: Generated vendor files
docs.text:
Target Result Vivado, interface with its own type A bus definition and abstraction definition XML pair under busdef/, one pair per type however many interfaces use it Vivado, generic ipcraft:busif:conduit:1.0 No bus interface: Vivado has no conduit concept, so the signals become plain ports in component.xml Quartus Platform Designer A conduit interface; the signals stay grouped, but Platform Designer does not connect them by protocol

Importing a component.xml back gives plain ports for a generic conduit, because the grouping cannot be recovered. Avalon-MM ports that Vivado's avalon_rtl does not declare (chipselect, debugaccess, and their active-low forms) are also plain ports in component.xml, but the importer folds them back into the Avalon-MM interface.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Vivado interface catalog: check whether Vivado already describes your protocol
  • Creating your first IP core: standard bus interfaces, clocks, resets, and ports

docs.title: Generating a vhdl_ls.toml
docs.text: The VHDL language server rust_hdl (the VHDL-LS extension) provides go to definition, find references and hover for VHDL, but only when its vhdl_ls.toml maps every source file to a VHDL library. IPCraft writes that file for you from the project files already in your repository, so names resolve across all IP cores.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The VHDL-LS extension, or vhdl_ls used by another editor
  • A trusted workspace (the command is not available in Restricted Mode)

docs.title: Generate the file
docs.text:
In VS Code, run IPCraft: Generate vhdl_ls.toml from the Command Palette. In a terminal, run:

ipcraft vhdl-ls [--root <dir>] [--dry-run] [--force]
Option Effect --root <dir> Folder to read and write vhdl_ls.toml in (default: the current directory) --dry-run Print the file instead of writing it --force Replace a vhdl_ls.toml that IPCraft did not write, after saving a backup

The file is written at the root of the folder. rust_hdl reads only that one file, so in a multi-root workspace IPCraft asks which folder to use.

IPCraft never runs on its own. Run the command again after you add a core, move files or rename a library. If rust_hdl does not pick up the new file, restart the language server.

docs.title: Where the libraries come from
docs.text:
IPCraft reads the files that state a library, in this order:

Source Library Vivado .xpr, Quartus .qsf and .qip The library of each file in the project component.xml The logicalName of each file _hw.tcl None; the files are known to belong to a core .ip.yml The logicalName of each file in fileSets, if set

Every other VHDL file in the folder goes into the library defaultlib, and so do files whose library is Vivado's xil_defaultlib or Quartus' work. use work.<unit> resolves the same way in defaultlib. Code that names xil_defaultlib explicitly (use xil_defaultlib.<unit>) does not resolve this way; IPCraft proposes the library instead (see below).

Generated output (*.gen, *.ip_user_files, .Xil, the synthesis and simulation folders Platform Designer writes next to a .qsys, and similar) is left out, so its copies do not collide with your sources.

When two files declare the same entity or package in one library, IPCraft keeps one: the one a project file or core names, otherwise the one with the shorter path. Between otherwise equal copies, one that needs a library IPCraft does not know (for example a nvc variant) loses. Template files that contain ${...} placeholders are never kept. The others appear as # excluded: comments in the file. An unlisted file whose units are all provided by a library in your user section (for example OSVVM deprecated/ copies) is excluded the same way, and your library wins, unless another file in the default library uses that copy.

Test environments often reuse names, for example one TestCtrl entity in each testbench folder, with test-case files that each bind to their own folder's copy. When files no project names declare the same unit in different folders, IPCraft gives each group of related folders a library of its own, named after the folder, and lists the files it needs from defaultlib in it too:

libraries.defaultlib_uart.files = [
  'uart/testbench/TestCtrl_e.vhd',  # unlisted
  'uart/TestCases/Tc1.vhd',  # unlisted
  'common/util_pkg.vhd',  # shared from defaultlib
]

A group that a file left in defaultlib depends on stays in defaultlib, so nothing there loses a unit. A test case written for a sibling testbench binds to the nearer folder.

When a file uses work.<unit> and only a file in another library declares that unit, the declaring file is also listed in the library of the file that uses it, marked # shared from <library>. The separate package body or architecture files of that unit come along, and so do the units it needs from the same library. A file is skipped when those would clash with a same-named unit the library already has from elsewhere. This covers defaultlib and the per-folder libraries, and also takes files from libraries you define in the user section, which IPCraft itself never changes.

docs.title: The user section
docs.text:
The end of vhdl_ls.toml is yours. IPCraft never changes what you write there, and settings such as standard = "2008" or a [lint] table belong there. A library you define there replaces the one IPCraft would generate.

When your code uses a library that IPCraft cannot find, such as osvvm, vunit_lib or unisim, it adds a commented proposal to the user section:

# Missing library osvvm, used by cores/uart/tb/uart_tb.vhd:5 and 3 other files.
# Packages it should provide were found in: ext/OsvvmLibraries/osvvm/
# [libraries.osvvm]
# files = ['ext/OsvvmLibraries/osvvm/*.vhd']
# exclude = ['ext/OsvvmLibraries/osvvm/OsvvmSettingsPkg_template.vhd']
# is_third_party = true

The exclude line lists files inside those folders that would break the library: files that add no unit beyond what another file already declares, template files, files another library of your user section already covers, and files a user exclude removed.

Check the path, remove the # from the [libraries...], files, exclude and is_third_party lines (the ones present), and run the command again. In VS Code, if the Vivado or Quartus installation is set in the IPCraft settings, proposals for vendor libraries such as unisim or altera_mf name the files in that installation; the CLI proposes a directory found in the workspace or a placeholder path instead.

docs.title: An existing vhdl_ls.toml
docs.text:
Existing file What happens Written by IPCraft and not edited outside the user section Replaced; the user section is kept Written by you, or IPCraft's part was edited IPCraft asks first (the CLI needs --force), saves a copy to .ipcraft/backup/, then writes a new file

The new file names the backup in its user section, so you can copy settings back.

docs.title: Generating a Project
docs.text: Scaffolding means creating a project structure from an IP core description. The selected scaffold pack controls the exact files.

docs.title: Generate the complete project
docs.text:
1. Open an .ip.yml file.
  2. Choose the HDL language, vendor targets, and scaffold pack in the toolbar.
  3. Run IPCraft: Scaffold Project (RTL + EDA packaging + Testbench).
  4. Review the staged files.
  5. Select Confirm and Apply.

Nothing is written before confirmation.

Staged state Meaning New File will be created Modified Existing content will change Unchanged No write is needed Protected User-owned file is excluded unless explicitly selected

Use View Diff on a modified file before accepting it. A protected file comes from a rule or file-set entry with managed: false. A file-set managed: false file is compared only once it exists on disk; before that IPCraft never generates it.

docs.title: Generate one part
docs.text:
Command Output Generate Top-Level HDL RTL selected by the pack Generate Cocotb Testbench Python tests and simulator files Generate Documentation Markdown supplied by the pack Generate Vivado Project Vivado Tcl scripts and constraints Generate Quartus Project Quartus Tcl script and constraints Generate Altera Platform Designer Component _hw.tcl component Generate Xilinx Vivado Component component.xml and XGUI files

Use a focused command when you intentionally want to leave other generated areas untouched.

docs.title: Review staged files
docs.text:
Each modified file has an action that decides what Confirm and Apply does with it. Hover a row to change it.

Action Effect Auto-merge Writes a three-way merge of the generator output into your edits. Offered only when the merge has no conflicts. Sync interface Replaces only the entity or module header (generics, ports) with the generated one and keeps everything else in your file. Offered for HDL files whose interface differs. Overwrite Replaces the file with the generated content. Keep Leaves the file on disk unchanged.

The default is Overwrite for unedited files and Auto-merge when your edits merge cleanly. It is Keep when your edits conflict with the generator output, when the generator output did not change, and for every protected (managed: false) file: a protected file is never written unless you pick another action yourself. Merge is separate: it opens the file in the three-way merge editor, and the file is then skipped by Apply.

Two badges explain why a file needs attention:

  • Hand-edited: the file differs from what IPCraft last generated.
  • Interface out of date: +N/-M/~K: the generated entity or module has N added, M removed, and K changed ports or generics compared with the file on disk. Hover the badge to list the names.

After Sync interface, the entity is up to date but new ports are not yet used. Connect them in the architecture or module body yourself.

IPCraft finds hand edits by comparing the file with a baseline, the content it last generated. Baselines are stored in .ipcraft/baseline/ inside the output folder, mirroring the generated paths. Commit this folder so teammates and CI share the same merge base. It is not listed in fileSets. Without a baseline (for example, the first run on an existing project), edits cannot be detected and a modified file defaults to Overwrite unless it is protected.

docs.title: Typical output
docs.text:
generated-core/
├── rtl/       HDL and register logic
├── tb/        generated tests
├── docs/      generated core documentation
├── xilinx/    Vivado packaging and project files
└── altera/    Quartus and Platform Designer files

Small scaffold packs may produce only one or two of these directories.

docs.title: Important settings
docs.text:
Setting Meaning ipcraft.generate.targets Vendor outputs to include ipcraft.generate.hdlLanguage VHDL or SystemVerilog ipcraft.generate.includeTestbench Whether complete scaffolding includes tests ipcraft.generate.includeDocs Whether complete scaffolding includes documentation ipcraft.generate.scaffoldPack Workspace fallback pack

The pack selected in the IP core takes priority over the workspace fallback.

docs.title: After generation
docs.text:
1. Review changes in version control.
  2. Add custom logic only to files intended to be user-owned.
  3. Compile the generated HDL.
  4. Run the generated tests.
  5. Run a Vivado or Quartus build when vendor files changed.

If a pack regenerates a file that users edit, mark that output managed: false before relying on it for hand-written logic.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Problem Check Empty or missing register logic Linked memory map and memoryMapRef Wrong bus wrapper Interface type and mode Vendor files missing Selected targets or vendor-specific command Template missing Pack's source name and built-in fallback Hand-written changes would be replaced Staging diff and managed: false Generated test misses RTL files Complete fileSets entries in the IP core

See the generator reference for output options and scaffold packs for custom layouts.

docs.title: Importing an Existing Design
docs.text: IPCraft can create an IP core description from VHDL, Quartus Platform Designer, or Vivado IP-XACT files. Import is a starting point: review the result before generating new files.

docs.title: Choose the source
docs.text: Source Command Result VHDL entity IPCraft: Import from VHDL (Experimental) .ip.yml Quartus _hw.tcl IPCraft: Import from Altera Platform Designer (Experimental) .ip.yml Vivado component.xml IPCraft: Import from Xilinx Component XML (Experimental) .ip.yml and sometimes .mm.yml

docs.title: Import VHDL
docs.text:
1. Open the Command Palette.
  2. Run IPCraft: Import from VHDL (Experimental).
  3. Select a .vhd or .vhdl file containing an entity.
  4. Review the new <entity-name>.ip.yml in the IP Core editor.

You can also run the command from the IPCraft menu or the title bar of an open VHDL file.

The importer reads:

VHDL content IPCraft result Entity name Core name Generics Parameters Clock-like ports Clocks Reset-like ports Resets and polarity Other ports Ports with direction and width Recognized bus signal groups Bus interfaces and physical prefixes

Bus detection compares signal groups with supported definitions. It can distinguish common AXI, AXI Stream, Avalon Memory-Mapped, and Avalon Streaming patterns, but naming conventions vary. Always check the chosen bus type and each signal mapping.

docs.title: Import Quartus Platform Designer metadata
docs.text:
1. Run IPCraft: Import from Altera Platform Designer (Experimental).
  2. Select the component's _hw.tcl file.
  3. Review the generated <component-name>.ip.yml.

The importer reads component metadata, parameters, ports, and interfaces that are explicitly described in the Tcl file. It does not import the complete Platform Designer system around the component.

docs.title: Import Vivado component metadata
docs.text:
1. Run IPCraft: Import from Xilinx Component XML (Experimental).
  2. Select component.xml.
  3. Review the generated <component-name>.ip.yml.

If the component contains memory-map information, IPCraft also creates a linked .mm.yml file. The importer does not recreate the surrounding Vivado block design.

docs.title: What import cannot determine reliably
docs.text:
Source files describe structure, but they do not always explain design intent. Review these items after every import:

  • vendor, library, name, and version;
  • clock and reset relationships;
  • bus type, mode, and signal mapping;
  • parameter limits and descriptions;
  • user-facing port descriptions;
  • links to memory maps;
  • special register behavior that is absent from the source metadata.

Do not assume a successful import means generated output is equivalent to the original project. Generate into a separate directory, review the staged files, and compile them before replacing any existing flow.

docs.title: Default identity settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Purpose ipcraft.import.vendor user Vendor assigned to imported cores; user may use the Git email domain ipcraft.import.library ip Default library ipcraft.import.version 1.0.0 Default version

VLNV is the four-part identity: vendor, library, name, and version.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Check consistency
  • Generate a project
  • Specification schemas

docs.title: Rendering Documentation Images
docs.text: Keep the diagrams in your documentation current by describing them once in a manifest and regenerating them with one command. The images are drawn from the same files the VS Code editors read, so they change only when a design does.

docs.title: Write the manifest
docs.text:
Create docs/images.yml next to the documentation. Paths are relative to this file.

defaults: { theme: light, scale: 2 }
images:
  - source: ../ip/axi_dma.ip.yml
    out: img/axi_dma.svg
  - source: ../bd/system.tcl
    out: img/system.png
    workspace: ../ip
  - source: ../bd/system.tcl
    out: img/dma-context.png
    select: [axi_dma_0]
    hops: 2
    workspace: ../ip
  - source: ../bd/system.tcl
    out: img/clocks.svg
    clocks: true

workspace points at the folder holding the .ip.yml and HDL files that define the blocks, so the image shows their pins as the system viewer does. Without it the design's own folder is searched.

docs.title: Render
docs.text:
ipcraft render --manifest docs/images.yml

Each image prints a Rendered line. If an entry has a mistake, it is reported with its position in the list (images[1] (../bd/system.tcl): ...), the other images are still written, and the command exits with 1, so a documentation build can fail on it.

Commit the images with the manifest. Running the command again gives the same bytes, so git diff shows only the diagrams whose design changed.

docs.title: Export from the editors
docs.text:
The system viewer and the IP core editor have an Export image button and the command IPCraft: Export Diagram as Image. They draw through the same renderer as ipcraft render, so an exported image with the Whole level (or Whole diagram) area equals what the command writes for the same design and options. Use the editors for one-off images, including Current view crops, and the command for images that must stay current in a documentation build. See Viewing a system design.

See the generator reference for every option.

docs.title: Reviewing System Design Changes in CI
docs.text:
The system-design-diff GitHub Action runs ipcraft diff on a pull request and posts the report as one comment, so a reviewer sees what a change did to a Vivado block design or a Platform Designer system without opening a vendor tool.

The action runs the IPCraft command line from a checkout of this repository that your workflow builds. It does not download anything else, and it needs no vendor tool.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A GitHub repository with the system design files (.bd, .tcl, .qsys) committed
  • A tag or commit of bleviet/ipcraft-vscode that has the diff command, which is a release after 1.5.3. Use the same tag or commit for the checkout of the command line and for the action, so the two match
  • A Linux or macOS runner. The action is tested there; it runs its scripts with bash

docs.title: Add the workflow
docs.text:
Create .github/workflows/system-design-diff.yml. Replace <tag-or-sha> with the tag or commit you chose:

name: System design diff

on: pull_request

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  diff:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Check out IPCraft
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          repository: bleviet/ipcraft-vscode
          ref: <tag-or-sha>
          submodules: true
          path: .ipcraft-cli

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Build the IPCraft command line
        working-directory: .ipcraft-cli
        run: |
          npm ci --ignore-scripts
          npx webpack --config config/webpack.config.js --config-name extension --config-name cli

      - uses: bleviet/ipcraft-vscode/actions/system-design-diff@<tag-or-sha>
        with:
          cli: .ipcraft-cli/dist/cli.js
          designs: |
            bd/system.bd
            qsys/soc.qsys

The build takes about half a minute. The webpack command builds the command line and copies the resources it reads at run time (bus definitions, schemas, fonts, the layout engine) into .ipcraft-cli/dist. npm run compile also works but builds the webviews too. submodules: true fetches the ipcraft-spec schemas the build needs.

fetch-depth: 0 on the first checkout makes the base revision of the pull request available to git. Without it ipcraft diff cannot read the base file and the run fails.

The action compares each design at the base of the pull request with the checked-out working tree, which is the merge result of the pull request. Pin the action and the command line to a tag or a commit, not to a branch, so a change in this repository cannot alter what runs with your token.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Input Default Meaning designs required Paths of the designs to compare, one per line or separated by spaces. A path cannot contain a space cli required Path to the built command line, dist/cli.js of the IPCraft checkout. The action fails with an error when the file does not exist base the base commit of the pull request Git revision to compare with. Required when the workflow does not run on a pull request: the action stops with an error when it is empty head the working tree Git revision to compare instead of the working tree fail-on not set changes or new-findings: fail the job when the check fails, see Fail the job ignore-version-only false Leave out blocks whose only change is the version of their IP comment true Post the report as a pull request comment github-token ${{ github.token }} Token used to post the comment

The action has two outputs: failed is true when a run failed its check or exited with an error, and report-dir is the folder with the files of the run: <n>.md (the report), <n>.exit (the exit code) and <n>.err (the error output) for the n-th design in designs.

docs.title: Fail the job
docs.text:
By default the job passes whether or not the designs differ. To make a pull request fail on a change, set fail-on:

      - uses: bleviet/ipcraft-vscode/actions/system-design-diff@<tag-or-sha>
        with:
          cli: .ipcraft-cli/dist/cli.js
          designs: bd/system.bd
          fail-on: new-findings

changes fails on any change, new-findings on at least one new finding, such as an undriven pin. The meaning is the one of --fail-on in the command line reference. Every design is compared even when an earlier one failed; the comment is posted, then the job fails.

docs.title: What the comment looks like
docs.text:
The comment holds the Markdown report of each design, one after the other, with the summary line, the findings, the address map, the external ports and one table per hierarchy level that changed. When a run failed its check, a line with the reason (for example Diff check failed: 3 changes (--fail-on changes)) follows its report. A design whose run wrote no report gets a heading and the last lines of its error output.

The action keeps one comment per pull request: each push updates it instead of adding a new one. Two uses of the action in one job, or two workflows, share that comment, and the last one to run replaces the content. Put all the designs of a pull request in one use of the action.

The comment is cut to fit the size limit of GitHub (65536 characters) with a note. The job summary of the run always has the full reports.

docs.title: Pull requests from forks
docs.text:
The action posts the comment only on the pull_request event. On a pull request from a fork the token of that event is read-only, so the comment cannot be posted: the action prints a warning and the job goes on. The reports are still written to the job summary of the run, and fail-on still decides whether the job passes.

Do not switch the workflow to pull_request_target to get a write token. That event runs in the context of the base repository with a write token and access to secrets, and the workflow would then check out and process the untrusted pull request with them. Posting the comment for fork pull requests from a separate workflow_run workflow is not supported by this action.

docs.title: Running a Cocotb Simulation
docs.text: Cocotb lets you test generated HDL with Python. IPCraft can generate the HDL, a Python test, and the files needed to start a simulator.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
You need:

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • pytest and cocotb
  • GHDL for VHDL, or Icarus Verilog for SystemVerilog

Install the Python packages:

python3 -m pip install cocotb pytest

Generate the project in IPCraft, open a terminal in the generated project, and run:

pytest -v tb/

docs.title: Generated files
docs.text:
The built-in packs write the tests to tb/:

generated-project/
├── rtl/                          # Generated VHDL or SystemVerilog
├── tb/
│   ├── <name>_test.py            # cocotb tests; extend this file
│   ├── test_<name>_sim.py        # one pytest function per cocotb test
│   ├── conftest.py               # compiles the HDL once per run
│   ├── register_model.py         # register model for memory-mapped cores
│   ├── verification_manifest.json
│   └── Makefile                  # make-based alternative to pytest
└── .vscode/settings.json         # points the Testing view at tb/

The register-map helper gives tests named access to registers and fields. This is clearer than repeating numeric addresses and masks throughout a test.

docs.title: Run tests
docs.text:
Run every test:

pytest -v tb/

Run one test:

pytest -v tb/ -k test_register_access

You can also run the cocotb Makefile directly:

make -C tb

docs.title: Choose a simulator
docs.text:
Cocotb reads the SIM environment variable. The default is the simulator selected when the testbench was generated. Examples:

SIM=ghdl pytest -v tb/
SIM=icarus pytest -v tb/

Use GHDL for generated VHDL and Icarus Verilog for generated SystemVerilog unless your scaffold pack documents another simulator.

docs.title: Read the result
docs.text:
A successful run reports each test as PASSED. A failed assertion includes the Python file and line number. Start with the first failure because later failures may be a consequence of it.

Generated tests may also produce a waveform file. Open it with a waveform viewer such as GTKWave to inspect signal changes over time.

docs.title: Use the VS Code Testing view
docs.text:
With the Python extension installed, VS Code can discover the generated pytest tests:

  1. Open the generated project folder.
  2. Open the Testing view.
  3. Choose Configure Python Tests if discovery has not run.
  4. Select pytest and the tb directory. The generated .vscode/settings.json already does this when you open the generated project as the workspace folder.
  5. Run or debug a test from the test tree.

The terminal command remains the best way to confirm the same tests work in automation.

docs.title: Write a custom register test
docs.text:
Generated memory-mapped testbenches expose a model (RegisterModel), a manifest, and an AxiTransport or AvalonTransport in tb/<ip_name>_test.py. Extend that file and look up registers and fields by name instead of repeating raw offsets and masks.

def test_register_layout():
    control = next(reg for reg in model.registers if reg["name"] == "CONTROL")
    assert control["offset"] == 0

    enable = next(field for field in control["fields"] if field["name"] == "ENABLE")
    assert enable["mask"] == 0x1

To extract or update a field in a register word:

enable_value = (register_value & enable["mask"]) >> enable["bitOffset"]
updated_value = (register_value & ~enable["mask"]) | (1 << enable["bitOffset"])

Keep layout checks separate from bus transactions. A layout test validates the generated register description; a cocotb coroutine validates the behavior of the simulated hardware.

docs.title: RTL sources are not found
docs.text: Run the test from the generated project root. Check that the paths in the generated Makefile or Python runner match the rtl/ directory.

docs.title: The simulator is not found
docs.text:
Confirm it is on PATH:

ghdl --version
iverilog -V

docs.title: Pytest finds no tests
docs.text: Pass the tb/ directory to pytest and run it from the generated project root. Only test_<name>_sim.py holds pytest functions; <name>_test.py holds the cocotb tests they start.

docs.title: GHDL rejects VHDL syntax
docs.text: Generated VHDL uses VHDL-2008. Make sure the generated runner passes --std=08 and that your GHDL version supports it.

docs.title: cocotb.runner cannot be imported
docs.text:
Check the installed version:

python3 -m pip show cocotb

Install the version required by the generated project or its requirements file.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• Generating a project
  • Memory-mapped registers
  • Generator reference

docs.title: Running the EDA Integration Tests
docs.text: These tests generate vendor project files and ask Quartus or Vivado to validate them. Run the suite for the vendor whose generator or templates you changed.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Install project dependencies first:

npm install

Then run one suite:

npm run test:integration:quartus
npm run test:integration:vivado

docs.title: Quartus
docs.text:
The Quartus suite runs through Docker. You need:

  • Docker running locally
  • Permission to start containers
  • The configured Quartus image available to Docker

docs.title: Vivado
docs.text:
The Vivado suite needs a local Vivado installation. The vivado command must be on PATH, or the configured Vivado path must point to it.

Both suites also need the ipcraft-spec submodule:

git submodule update --init --recursive

docs.title: What each suite checks
docs.text:
Suite What it proves Quartus project check Generated Tcl and project settings can be read by Quartus Quartus testbench check Generated bus test code compiles with the generated design Vivado IP check Generated IP-XACT metadata passes Vivado's integrity checks Vivado block-design check The generated IP can be placed and connected in a block design

These tests are slower than unit tests because they start external tools. They are intentionally separate from npm test.

docs.title: Skip a missing tool
docs.text: If you have only one vendor tool, run only that vendor's command. Do not treat a locally unavailable tool as proof that its generated output is valid; rely on the matching CI job or ask another contributor to run it.

docs.title: Read the output
docs.text:
A successful run names each generated example and ends with a passing Jest summary. A skipped check states which tool or optional stage was unavailable.

For a failure:

  1. Find the first vendor error, not the final Jest summary.
  2. Note the generated example and output path.
  3. Re-run only the failing suite.
  4. Compare the generated file with the source template in src/generator/templates/.

Do not edit files under dist/; they are copied from the source templates during the build.

docs.title: Docker cannot start
docs.text:
Confirm Docker is running:

docker info

Then confirm the configured Quartus image is present or can be pulled.

docs.title: No Quartus examples were generated
docs.text: Check that the test inputs include an Altera or Intel target and that the generator completed before Docker started.

docs.title: No Vivado examples were generated
docs.text: Check that the test inputs include an AMD target and that Vivado generation is enabled for the selected example.

docs.title: Vivado cannot be started
docs.text:
Run:

vivado -version

If that fails, add Vivado's bin directory to PATH or update the project setting that points to Vivado.

docs.title: A test times out
docs.text: Check whether the vendor process is still active. First runs are often slower because tools create caches. If the process is stuck, inspect the vendor log in the generated output directory.

docs.title: Generated output looks stale
docs.text: Remove only the suite's temporary generated-output directory, rebuild, and rerun the test. Do not edit cached output to fix a template problem.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• How EDA integration tests work
  • Testing

docs.title: Using the Data Inspector
docs.text: The Data Inspector turns a pasted or captured value into named fields. It does not change the IP core, memory map, or generated hardware.

docs.title: Start with the right command
docs.text:
Goal Command Inspect a temporary value IPCraft: Open Data Inspector Decode a known register or port IPCraft: Open Register or Port in Data Inspector Save and reuse a setup IPCraft: New Data Inspector

A saved setup uses an .ipci.yml recipe file.

docs.title: Four simple terms
docs.text:
• A sample is the temporary value you paste or load.
  • A source gives that value a stable name and width.
  • An operation creates a new value by combining or changing sources.
  • A field gives a bit range a name and display format.

Recipes save sources, operations, fields, and view preferences. They do not save pasted values or capture history.

docs.title: Inspect one value
docs.text:
1. Run IPCraft: Open Data Inspector.
  2. Paste a value into Literal.
  3. Set Width if the value does not include one.
  4. Select Decode.

Accepted forms include:

Style Example Verilog hexadecimal 32'hDEAD_BEEF Verilog binary 16'b0000_XXXX_0011_ZZZZ VHDL hexadecimal x"0123_ABCD" VHDL binary b"1010_0011" C-style hexadecimal 0xDEADBEEF C-style binary 0b10100011 Decimal 3735928559 with an explicit width

X means unknown and Z means high impedance. The inspector preserves both states instead of treating them as zero.

docs.title: Read the bit view
docs.text:
The most significant bit is on the left; bit 0 is on the right. For wide values:

  • choose a lane width of 8, 16, 32, or 64 bits;
  • use overview, field, or bit zoom;
  • use Jump to bit to reach one position;
  • use arrow keys, Home, and End between lanes.

The band above the bits shows which source supplied each range. Field overlays name decoded ranges. Inserted, masked, and dropped ranges remain visible in the operation details.

docs.title: Decode a memory-mapped register
docs.text:
1. Run IPCraft: Open Register or Port in Data Inspector.
  2. Choose a register.
  3. Paste the captured value.
  4. Select Decode.
  5. Open Fields to review each range.

The import copies field names, ranges, descriptions, and known values. It does not edit or stay linked to the .mm.yml file.

To decode a port instead, choose it from the same list. Ports come from the fields metadata in .ip.yml files: top-level ports, conduit ports, and bus interface ports (portFields). The width is the port width resolved with parameter defaults, and the import never edits the .ip.yml file.

Choose an interpretation for each field:

Interpretation Use Hex or binary Raw bits, including X or Z Unsigned Counts and sizes Signed Two's-complement values Enum Named modes or states Float 16-, 32-, or 64-bit IEEE-754 values Fixed point Signed values with a chosen number of fractional bits

An expected value adds a pass, fail, or unknown comparison.

docs.title: Add fields manually
docs.text:
Use manual fields when no register describes the value:

  1. Select Add field.
  2. Set its name, highest bit, and lowest bit.
  3. Choose an interpretation.
  4. Repeat for the remaining ranges.

Fields in one overlay group cannot overlap. Create another group when you need two valid interpretations of the same bits, such as four bytes and one 32-bit signed value.

docs.title: Combine or change values
docs.text:
Use the Library to add another source or an operation.

Operation Result Concat Put one value above another Slice Keep one inclusive bit range AND, OR, XOR, NOT Apply bit logic Shift left or right Shift within the same width and insert zeros Zero or sign extend Increase width Truncate Keep the low bits at a smaller width Byte swap Reverse bytes in a byte-aligned value

For example, to build a 64-bit value from two 32-bit sources:

  1. Name the first source ADDR_HI.
  2. Add a source named ADDR_LO.
  3. Add Concat.
  4. Connect ADDR_HI to the high input and ADDR_LO to the low input.

A new operation stays dashed until every required input is connected. Select any node to show its result in the bit view.

A connected operation can still report a problem, most often when a binary operation joins two different widths. The operation stays on the canvas and names the failing rule, the Problems counter includes it, and the recipe is not saved until you fix it. Select the source you want to change and correct its width in the Inspector; the operation starts evaluating as soon as the widths agree.

docs.title: Inspect a VCD waveform
docs.text:
1. Select a source.
  2. Open Capture in the Inspector.
  3. Choose a VCD file and one or more signals.
  4. Select Index selected signals.
  5. Move through samples with Previous, Next, or the slider.

VCD is a waveform file format used by HDL simulators. Selecting several signals creates several sources; add Concat when they form one logical value.

docs.title: Inspect CSV, ILA, or SignalTap data
docs.text:
Use capture import when a CSV file contains several samples of the same signal. The Data Inspector supports plain CSV files, Vivado ILA exports, and Quartus SignalTap exports.

  1. Run IPCraft: Open Data Inspector.
  2. Enter an initial value with the same width as the captured signal.
  3. Select Decode.
  4. Select Capture, then open CSV / ILA / SignalTap capture.
  5. Choose or paste a CSV file.
  6. Select the signal column and number base.
  7. Set word width, word order, and byte order.
  8. Select Import samples, then use the timeline to move between samples.

The initial value only sets the source width and opens the workspace. Imported samples replace it as you move along the timeline.

Word order rearranges complete words. Byte order rearranges bytes inside each word. Set both to match the capture file before adding transform operations.

docs.title: Try the sample capture files
docs.text:
Use the example closest to your capture:

Capture source Example file What it shows Script, test, or firmware log generic-status.csv Selecting a signal column Vivado ILA vivado-ila-address.csv Ignoring Vivado metadata columns Quartus SignalTap signaltap-bus.csv Preserving unknown X and Z bits

All three examples use these settings:

Setting Value Number base Hexadecimal Byte order Big endian Word order High word first Word width 8

docs.title: Generic status trace
docs.text:
Start with 32'h00000000, then import generic-status.csv. Select STATUS as the signal column. The sample column is a label, so do not select it as the signal.

Add these fields to check the result:

Name Bits Display BUSY [0:0] Unsigned FIFO_LEVEL [15:4] Unsigned FSM_STATE [18:16] Unsigned or enum Raw value BUSY FIFO_LEVEL FSM_STATE 0x00000000 0 0 0 0x00031211 1 289 3 0x00043220 0 802 4 0x00010001 1 0 1

docs.title: Vivado ILA address trace
docs.text:
Start with 32'h00000000, then import vivado-ila-address.csv. The Data Inspector recognizes Sample in Buffer and Sample in Window as Vivado metadata and offers ADDR as the signal column.

Add a PAGE field for bits [31:12] and an OFFSET field for bits [11:0]. The first four samples stay on page 0x12 and move through four-byte offsets. The last sample is page 0x13, offset 0xF00.

docs.title: SignalTap trace with unknown bits
docs.text:
Start with 16'h0000, then import signaltap-bus.csv. The Data Inspector recognizes Data: and Time: as SignalTap metadata and offers BUS as the signal column.

Add these fields:

Name Bits Display UPPER_BYTE [15:8] Hexadecimal STATE [7:4] Unsigned or enum FLAGS [3:0] Binary

At 0xXXA5, UPPER_BYTE is unknown, while STATE and FLAGS still decode because their bits are known. At 0xZZZZ, the binary view keeps the Z bits and numeric fields show that the value is unknown.

docs.title: Check word and byte order
docs.text:
For a 32-bit captured value of 12345678, set Word width to 16 and compare the preview:

Byte order Word order Imported result Big endian High word first 32'h12345678 Big endian Low word first 32'h56781234 Little endian High word first 32'h34127856

Choose the settings that describe the capture file. If an unrelated transform is needed to make the value look correct, check the import settings again.

For your own capture, keep one header row, use one number base in the selected column, and choose a source width large enough for every value. The source width must be divisible by the word width. Keep X and Z digits when the capture contains unknown states.

The Data Inspector imports one signal column at a time. To combine signals, add them as named sources and use Concat.

docs.title: Save and share the setup
docs.text:
From a temporary inspector, select Save recipe. To start with an empty saved recipe, run IPCraft: New Data Inspector.

After reopening a recipe, paste or load a new sample. The saved field and operation structure is applied to that new data.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Problem Check Decimal input is rejected Set Width Field is invalid Confirm 0 <= lowest bit <= highest bit < source width Numeric value is unknown The field contains X or Z; use hex or binary Fields overlap Move one field or use another overlay group Bitwise operation fails Both inputs must have the same width Byte swap fails Width must be divisible by eight Capture appears reversed Check word width, then word order, then byte order Added source has no value Select it, enter a sample, and choose Set

For implementation and exact bit-state rules, see the Data Inspector concept.

docs.title: Using Arithmetic Functions in Port Widths
docs.text:
A parameter is a value chosen when the core is integrated. A width expression uses that parameter to calculate a port width automatically. For example, a FIFO with 1024 entries needs 10 address bits because clog2(1024) is 10.

A port width may be a literal integer, a parameter name, or an arithmetic expression. Expressions may use the following predefined functions:
