When several files match, the one nearest the design file wins; a tie is left undefined. The search follows symbolic links (not into a loop), skips node_modules, .git, .Xil and Vivado-generated folders (*.gen, *.cache, *.ip_user_files, *.runs, *.sim) anywhere in a path relative to the workspace folder (the viewer applies the same filter to the whole path), reads at most 2000 .ip.yml, 5000 HDL and 2000 .qsys files, the first by sorted relative path, and ignores HDL files over 1 MiB. VS Code's files.exclude setting is not applied. Without a match the block is drawn as the design declares it, so a design with no definitions nearby gives the same image with or without --workspace. Use --no-workspace for that image on purpose. A folder or an invalid .ip.yml that is skipped is reported as a warning on stderr.

The command reads those files without asking for trust, like generate; point --workspace only at folders you trust. Display names are relative to the workspace folder, and the result does not depend on file system order.

docs.title: Render many images from one manifest
docs.text:
ipcraft render --manifest docs/images.yml renders every entry of a YAML file. Paths are relative to the manifest file.

defaults: { theme: light, scale: 2, legend: true }
images:
  - source: ip/axi_dma.ip.yml
    out: docs/img/axi_dma.svg
  - source: bd/system.tcl
    out: docs/img/dma-context.png
    select: [axi_dma_0]
    hops: 2
    workspace: ip

Each entry takes source and out (required) and the options level, expand, select, hops, highlight, clocks, theme, scale, quality, grid, legend, background and workspace (a folder, or false for none). expand, select and highlight are lists or comma-separated strings; clocks, grid and legend are true or false. defaults takes the same keys except source and out, which every image sets itself, and applies under every entry. A default that an entry cannot use is skipped: scale for an SVG, quality for a non-JPG, background: transparent for a JPG, hops without select, and the system design options (level, expand, select, hops, highlight, clocks, legend, workspace) for an .ip.yml. A key set on the entry itself is checked like the matching flag, with the same message. An unknown key is an error, as are an empty images list and two images with the same out. workspace: false (or null) draws that design without workspace definitions, like --no-workspace.

The images are rendered one after another in file order, sharing the fonts, the rasterizer, the bus library and the workspace file lists. Each success prints Rendered <path>. An entry that fails prints images[<index>] (<source>): <message> on stderr and the others still render; the exit code is 1 if any failed, 0 otherwise. A problem with the manifest as a whole (unreadable file, invalid YAML, unknown top-level key) renders nothing and exits with 1. Output folders are created. An image from a manifest is byte for byte the image the same options give on the command line.

docs.title: Compare two revisions of a system design
docs.text:
diff reports what changed between two revisions of a system design, in terms of blocks, parameters, connections, external ports and the address map. It reads a Vivado block design .tcl or .bd, a Platform Designer .qsys or a qsys-script .tcl, and needs no VS Code window. The text of the files is not compared; the two designs are read into the viewer's graph and the graphs are compared, so the order of blocks and nets, net names, line numbers and tool metadata do not show up as changes.

There are two forms:

# one file: the working tree (or --head) against a git revision
ipcraft diff bd/system.bd --base HEAD
ipcraft diff bd/system.bd --base main --head feature/fifo

# two files on disk
ipcraft diff old/system.qsys new/system.qsys

# fail a CI job when a pull request adds findings
ipcraft diff bd/system.bd --base origin/main --fail-on new-findings
Option Meaning --base <git ref> One-file form. The revision to compare with: a branch, tag, commit or HEAD~1. The file is read at the same path in the repository that contains it, or under its old path when git finds that it was renamed since (see below) --head <git ref> One-file form, with --base. Compare with this revision instead of the working tree --format <markdown\|json> Report format (default markdown) --out <file> Write the report to this file instead of standard output. The folder is created if needed --ignore-version-only Leave out blocks whose only change is the version of their IP. The JSON report then has no instance with status version and summary.version is 0 --fail-on <changes\|new-findings> Exit with 1 when the check fails: changes on any change (the total of the summary, after --ignore-version-only; a difference of findings alone is not a change), new-findings on at least one new finding (resolved findings never fail) --image <file.svg\|png\|jpg> Also draw the top level of the current revision with the changes marked, to this file; the extension picks the format. The folder is created if needed

--image draws what the viewer shows with Marks on, at the top level / of the current revision with nothing expanded, in the look ipcraft render has by default (light theme, grid, legend, editor background, scale 2). Added blocks, blocks with changed parameters or pins, renamed and moved blocks, blocks with only a new version and added or changed external ports have a border in the color of their kind and a sign in the header (+, ~, →, », v); a hierarchy with changes inside has a ~ N inside count; the pins that gained or changed a connection have their name in color; new wires are drawn in the added color, a little wider. The blocks and ports that only the base has are drawn as ghosts, as the viewer draws them with Show removed on: a dashed border in the removed color, the name struck through, a − in the header and a dimmed body; a pin a block lost has its name struck through, and a lost wire is dashed in the removed color. The image is laid out with both revisions, so a block can sit somewhere else than in an image of the current revision alone. The legend names the kinds present, including − Removed, and Removed wire when there is one. With --ignore-version-only, blocks with only a version change are not marked. For another level, an expanded hierarchy or another look, use the viewer. The command prints Wrote <file> on its own line after the report: to standard output when the report is written with --out, to standard error when the report is on standard output, so the report stays clean. --fail-on still decides the exit code, after the image is written. An image that cannot be drawn or written also exits with 1 and prints Image failed: <reason>; the report is still written.

ipcraft diff bd/system.bd --base main --image docs/img/changes.png

Without --fail-on, the exit code is 0 when the report is written, whether or not the designs differ. It is 1 on an error (an option error, a file or revision that cannot be read, or a file that is not a system design) or when --fail-on fails the check, and when --image cannot be drawn or written. The report is written or printed first in every case, so a CI job can fail and still keep it. A failed image prints Image failed: <reason> to standard error, before any failed check. A failed check prints one line to standard error, for example Diff check failed: 3 changes (--fail-on changes) or Diff check failed: 1 new finding (--fail-on new-findings). In a CI job:

ipcraft diff bd/system.bd --base origin/main --out diff.md --fail-on new-findings

The Markdown report is made for a pull request comment:

## System design changes: zynq_gpio_system

Comparing `HEAD` (base) with `working tree`.

**+1 added · −4 removed · ~2 changed · v1 version only · 0 new findings · 1 resolved finding**

### Findings
| | Finding | Where | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resolved | undriven pin | `led_o` | |

Findings are computed from the design files alone; workspace definitions are not used, so pins of blocks without a known pin list are not checked.

### Address map
| | Address space | Segment | Base | Current |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| − | `sys_ps7/Data` | `axi_gpio_0/S_AXI/Reg` | `0x41200000` · `0x00010000` | |
| ~ | `sys_ps7/Data` | `gpio_block/axi_gpio_1/S_AXI/Reg` | `0x41210000` · `0x00010000` | `0x41220000` · `0x00010000` |

### External ports
| | Port | Base | Current |
|---|---|---|---|
| − | `led_o` | direction `out` · width `7:0` · not connected | |

### Level `/`
| | Block | Change | Base | Current |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| + | `axis_data_fifo_0` | added | | `xilinx.com:ip:axis_data_fifo:2.0` |
| + | `axis_data_fifo_0` | pin `s_axis_aclk` connects to | | `sys_ps7/FCLK_CLK1` |
| ~ | `sys_ps7` | parameter `CONFIG.PCW_FPGA0_PERIPHERAL_FREQMHZ` | `100` | `150` |

### Level `/gpio_block`
| | Block | Change | Base | Current |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v | `axi_gpio_1` | version | `xilinx.com:ip:axi_gpio:2.0` | `xilinx.com:ip:axi_gpio:2.1` |

The Findings section lists what the review of the viewer (the Unconnected and Clocks tabs) reports in one revision and not in the other: New for a finding only the current revision has, Resolved for one only the base has. A finding is one of

  • an undriven pin or an unused pin, a pin that no net touches on its level. An undriven pin is one that something should drive: an input of a block, or an output of the design or of a hierarchy, seen from inside. An unused pin is any other pin that no net touches: an output of a block, an input of the design or of a hierarchy, or an inout or a pin without a direction. Its Where is instanceName/pin for a block, or the pin name for a pin of the design or of a hierarchy;
  • a data crossing or a reset crossing: a connection or a reset whose two ends are on different clock domains with no known synchronizer; its Where is from → to, and its Detail the two clocks and the reason. Crossings that Vivado times (related clocks), crossings that are unchecked because a clock is not known, blocks that span domains, and crossings that are fine are not findings. A Platform Designer system (.qsys, qsys-script) has no crossing findings, because Platform Designer inserts the clock crossing adapters itself.

A finding is the same in both revisions when it is the same pin (or the same two ends), so a renamed net does not make a new finding. A renamed block keeps its findings: they are neither new nor resolved, and a resolved finding that mentions it uses the new name. The section is written when at least one finding differs, and the summary line then ends with N new findings · M resolved findings; when only findings differ the report is the summary and this section rather than No changes. --ignore-version-only does not filter findings. As in the viewer, a pin is checked only when the design files list the pins of its block, and workspace definitions are not used, so pins of blocks without a known pin list are not checked (the note under the table says so). The JSON report has the same lists in a findings field, { "new": [...], "resolved": [...] }, empty when nothing differs; each entry has kind (undriven, unused, dataCrossing, resetCrossing), level, and for a pin instance (null for a boundary pin), pin and label, for a crossing from, to, fromInstance and toInstance (the instance path of each end, null for an external port or a reset whose source is not known), fromClock, toClock (left out when the clock is not known) and reason, sorted by kind, level and label.

Each sign has a meaning: + added, − removed, ~ changed, → renamed, » moved, v version only. A section without changes is left out, and a report without any change reads No changes. Connections are compared per pin: a pin whose set of connected pins changed is listed with the old and the new set (not connected for an empty set), however the nets are named. Only the pin that moved is listed: a pin whose net gained or lost a neighbour is not reported when the neighbour is a pin of an added or removed block, and not when its other connections stayed and the neighbour is the pin that joined or left (a new signal on an existing net lists the new pin, not every pin on that net). A new or removed block lists its own connected pins. A pin that is connected to a pin on another level of the hierarchy (a net of the top level can name a pin of a block inside a hierarchy) is written with its absolute path, such as /a/x. For a hierarchy block /h/g1, /h/g1/z is its pin z seen from outside and /h/g1:z is the same pin seen from inside. The pins of a hierarchy block are compared from the outside and from the inside: a row such as pin `fin` inside connects to lists what the pin is connected to within the hierarchy, with the names relative to that hierarchy (fifo/s_axis there is the block fifo inside it), and only the pin that moved is listed there too. The attributes (direction, signal type, interface, width) and parameters of external ports and of the pins of a hierarchy block are compared too, one row per difference; a direction is compared only when both revisions declare it. For the pins of other blocks only the connections are compared. The JSON report is the same change list as data; a changed pin or port also carries gained and lost, the sorted peers (written like currentPeers and basePeers) that only the current revision or only the base has, left out when empty, so a renamed block is neither.

A block is identified by its path, so a renamed block would be one removed and one added block. In every format (Vivado .bd and write_bd_tcl script, Platform Designer .qsys and qsys-script), the diff pairs them as a rename only when they are the same block under a new name: the same level, kind, type (version included), parameters and pin names, and, after the rename is applied to the base, the diff reports no change on the block (for a hierarchy: nor on anything inside it). Connections to blocks that were added or removed, and neighbours that only joined or left one of its nets, do not count as a change of the block. There must be exactly one such removed and one such added block in the level, so identical candidates are not guessed at, and the pairs are checked together, so the result does not depend on names. A renamed block is one row, with the characters that differ in bold, and the address segments and the connections of other blocks that only differed by the name are not reported; the Base column shows the names the base had. A block whose address changed is still a rename, and its segment is shown as changed under the new name. A block that is renamed and also changed stays removed plus added, and a block moved to another level is not a rename. In JSON, a rename is an instance with status renamed, path (the new path), basePath (the old one), empty parameters and pins, and is counted in summary.renamed. The summary line of the Markdown report adds →N renamed when N is not 0:

| → | `framebuffer_reader` | renamed | `frambuffer_reader` | `fram`**`e`**`buffer_reader` |

After the renames, a removed and an added block are paired as a move when they are the same block under another parent level: the same name, kind, type (version included), parameters and pin names, each the topmost block of its subtree (neither lies below another removed or added block), and the only such pair. All pairs are applied to the base at once, with the block and what is below it under the new path and the nets staying on their levels, so the pins of the moved block can see other neighbours. A pair is kept when nothing differs below the moved block and the block itself has no change but its pins (no parameter, type or attribute change); the others stay removed plus added, as does a block that is moved and renamed, or moved into a hierarchy that is itself new. A move is one row in the new level, with the old path under Base and the new path under Current, followed by the rows of the pins whose connections changed, written as for a changed block; the pins of the blocks that were connected to it are listed from their side, as for any rewired pin. In JSON, a move is an instance with status moved, path (the new path), basePath (the old one), level (the new parent level), empty parameters and the changed pins, and is counted in summary.moved; summary has the key with 0 when there is no move. The summary line of the Markdown report adds »N moved when N is not 0, and --fail-on changes counts a move as a change:

| » | `framebuffer_reader` | moved | `/framebuffer_reader` | `/video/framebuffer_reader` |
| ~ | `framebuffer_reader` | pin `M_AXI` connects to | `axi_interconnect_0/S00_AXI` | `S_AXI_FB` |

If the two files are of different formats, for example a write_bd_tcl script and a .bd of the same design, the report says so, because each format knows different things about the design (a .bd declares the pins of module references, a script lists only the pins it connects).

Both revisions are read as text and nothing is executed, as in the viewer. The revision is read from the local git object store with git show; there is no network access and nothing is checked out.

A file that was added after the base revision, or that had another path there, is still compared. If the file is not at the same path in the base revision, diff asks git for the renames between the base and the current side (git diff-index -M for the working tree, git diff-tree -M for --head, at the default similarity of git; your diff.* settings do not apply) and reads the file under its old path; a file that was also edited since is paired with its old self as long as git pairs them. The report says so in one line after the Comparing line:

Read at HEAD~1 as `bd/old_name.bd` (renamed since).

If git finds no such rename and the path is not in the tree of the base revision, the file did not exist there, and the base is an empty design: every block, port and address segment is added, the line reads

The file did not exist at HEAD~1: everything is added.

and --fail-on changes fails on the added blocks. --fail-on new-findings fails too when the new file has any finding (an unconnected pin, a clock or reset crossing), because every finding of a file that was not there before is new. In the JSON report, base has "path": "bd/old_name.bd" (relative to the repository root) for a renamed file and "missing": true for a file that did not exist; neither field is there otherwise. A rename is found only for a file that git knows: a new name that is not added to the index is not paired with the old file. The current side must exist: a file that is not in the working tree (or at --head) is an error, and so is any other failure of git, with git's own reason, also a path that is in the base revision whose content git cannot read (a partial clone without its remote, say).

Limits for now: workspace definitions (.ip.yml, HDL, .qsys) are not used, so only the pins the design files list are compared; the viewer's comparison reads the definitions of a base revision from git, ipcraft diff does not. The path given to git show is the spelling on the command line, so on a case-insensitive file system a path with the wrong case is found on disk but not at the revision, so the file is reported as new, with everything added, rather than as an error. A file stored with Git LFS is read as its pointer text and reported as not a recognized system design. The concept is in System Design Diff.

docs.title: Upgrade files to the latest format
docs.text:
An .ip.yml declares its file format version in apiVersion (1.0, 1.1, or 1.2); a file without apiVersion is version 1.0. IPCraft reads every version up to its latest (1.2), refuses a file that declares a newer version with an error asking you to upgrade IPCraft, and can upgrade older files. Version 1.1 introduced bus interface contracts: legacy port names such as Avalon-MM read_n or waitrequest_n become one port plus an entry in portPolarityOverrides. Version 1.2 added port field metadata and changes no existing content. The IP Core editor applies this upgrade (and sets apiVersion: '1.2') when you make the first edit to an older file; to upgrade explicitly, run:

ipcraft migrate path/to/core.ip.yml other.ip.yml
ipcraft migrate path/to/core.ip.yml --check
ipcraft migrate path/to/map.mm.yml

Each file is rewritten in place only when it changes, preserving comments and hex literals; the command prints Upgraded <path> (1.0 -> 1.2, <n> change(s)) or Up to date: <path> (1.2). With --check nothing is written, files that need an upgrade are listed as Needs upgrade: <path> (1.0 -> 1.2), and the exit status is 1 if any file would change (useful in CI). A file that cannot be read or parsed, or that declares a newer version, is reported and makes the exit status 1, but the remaining files are still processed. The bus library honors useBusLibrary from each file.

In VS Code, the same migration is available as IPCraft: Migrate .ip.yml / .mm.yml to Latest Format, from the Explorer context menu (multi-select is supported) or the Command Palette for the active .ip.yml or .mm.yml. Like ipcraft migrate, it also converts legacy keys in .mm.yml files and repairs a dangling memoryMapRef. It applies one undoable edit per file and saves it. If a file already has unsaved changes in the editor, the upgrade is applied to the open buffer but the file is not saved, so your unrelated edits are not written to disk unasked; the summary message reports how many files were left unsaved.

docs.title: Convert legacy snake_case keys
docs.text: IPCraft reads camelCase keys only. Old files may still use snake_case spellings such as address_blocks, base_address, address_offset, reset_value, memory_maps, file_sets, use_optional_ports or physical_prefix. Run ipcraft migrate to convert them. It works for .ip.yml and .mm.yml files, renames the keys in place, and keeps comments, key order and hex literals. For an .ip.yml file the conversion runs together with the version upgrade, and a file that is already at the latest version is still rewritten when it has legacy keys. If a node has both spellings, the camelCase key wins and the legacy key is removed. A .mm.yml file has no apiVersion, so only keys are renamed. In an .ip.yml file, ipcraft migrate also rewrites a dot-separated bus type such as ipcraft.busif.axi4_lite.1.0 (the spelling the IPCraft Python CLI uses) to its colon VLNV ipcraft:busif:axi4_lite:1.0 when that VLNV resolves in the active bus library, at any format version. The VS Code Migrate command handles .ip.yml files the same way.

docs.title: Generate a vhdl_ls.toml
docs.text:
ipcraft vhdl-ls --root . --dry-run

--dry-run prints the file instead of writing it, and --force replaces a vhdl_ls.toml that IPCraft did not write (the old file is saved to .ipcraft/backup/). See Generating a vhdl_ls.toml.

docs.title: Build the npm package
docs.text:
The standalone ipcraft npm package remains unpublished and separate. Contributors can build a local package archive and install it in a clean environment:

npm run package:cli
npm install --global ./build/ipcraft-<version>.tgz
ipcraft generate path/to/core.ip.yml --target quartus --lang vhdl --out gen/

docs.title: Commands & Settings Reference
docs.text: Use this page to look up every IPCraft command and setting. Start with the common tasks below; the later tables are the complete reference.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text:
Goal Command Create a core and linked register map IPCraft: New IP Core + Register Map Generate the complete project IPCraft: Scaffold Project (RTL + EDA packaging + Testbench) Check generated files against the specification IPCraft: Check Consistency Import an existing VHDL entity IPCraft: Import from VHDL (Experimental) Run the available vendor build IPCraft: Build Switch from the visual editor to YAML IPCraft: Open as Text Editor

All commands are in the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P). A blank cell in the location tables means the command is not available there.

docs.title: Command map
docs.text: The diagram groups every command by workflow stage. Follow the arrows from creating or importing a specification to generating, validating, and building. Ctrl+Shift+V (Cmd+Shift+V on macOS) is context-sensitive: on a VHDL, Verilog, SystemVerilog, _hw.tcl, or component.xml file it opens a read-only preview from which you can save an .ip.yml; on an .ip.yml or .mm.yml file it switches between the text and visual editors; on a Vivado block design .tcl script or .bd file, a Platform Designer .qsys file, or a Platform Designer system script it opens or closes the read-only system diagram. The editable source is commands-map.drawio.

docs.title: Workspace Trust and Restricted Mode
docs.text:
IPCraft has limited support for untrusted workspaces. In Restricted Mode, the visual IP Core, Memory Map, and Data Inspector editors remain available for local authoring. The following inspection features also remain available and do not execute workspace content:

  • view built-in bus definitions and scan workspace bus-definition files;
  • run HDL and full consistency checks, which only parse project files;
  • copy a component instance, switch between text and visual editors, and view existing build output;
  • create or migrate IPCraft YAML files and open IPCraft help and settings.

Commands that render templates, generate output, invoke Git during import, scan an installed vendor catalog, build a project, or launch Vivado, Quartus, or Platform Designer are disabled until the workspace is trusted. Calls from the Command Palette, extension API, and IPCraft webviews use the same trust check. If a command is invoked programmatically in Restricted Mode, IPCraft shows an error with an option to open VS Code's Workspace Trust management.

Workspace values for scaffold-pack selection and paths, vendor runners, installation directories, and Docker images are ignored in Restricted Mode. Trust the workspace only when you are comfortable allowing its templates, generated scripts, and tool configuration to run on your machine.

docs.title: All commands
docs.text: All commands are available in the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) under the IPCraft category. Many commands are also reachable from the IPCraft top-level application menu bar entry or from the editor title bar icon.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Command Palette IPCraft Menu Editor Title IPCraft: New IP Core Yes Yes IPCraft: New Register Map Yes Yes IPCraft: New IP Core + Register Map Yes Yes

New IP Core — Creates a new .ip.yml file with a minimal VLNV skeleton and opens it in the IP Core visual editor.

New Register Map — Creates a new .mm.yml file with an empty address block and opens it in the Memory Map visual editor.

New IP Core + Register Map — Creates both files at once and links them via a memoryMapRef bus interface.

docs.title: Scaffold & Generate
docs.text:
These commands are available on .ip.yml files.

Command Palette IPCraft Menu Editor Title IPCraft: Scaffold Project (RTL + EDA packaging + Testbench) Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Generate Top-Level HDL Yes IPCraft: Generate CocoTB Testbench Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Generate Vivado Project Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Generate Quartus Project Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Generate Altera Platform Designer Component (_hw.tcl) Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Generate Xilinx Vivado Component (component.xml) Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Generate & Build (Vivado OOC) Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Generate & Build (Quartus) Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Generate Documentation Yes Yes Yes

Scaffold Project — The all-in-one command. Generates RTL files (VHDL or SystemVerilog, controlled by ipcraft.generate.hdlLanguage), a testbench, and vendor project files in a single step. Part number and device are read from settings (ipcraft.vivado.defaultPart, ipcraft.quartus.defaultDevice). The output is written next to the .ip.yml file.

Generate Top-Level HDL — Generates RTL source files only (package, top entity, core skeleton, bus wrapper, register file). Prompts for an output directory. Respects ipcraft.generate.hdlLanguage.

Generate CocoTB Testbench — Generates the testbench scaffold in the tb/ directory. The framework and simulator engine are controlled by ipcraft.testbench.framework and ipcraft.testbench.engine. See Run cocotb Simulations for details.

Generate Vivado Project — Prompts for an FPGA part number, then generates xilinx/<ip_name>_project.tcl (OOC project creator), xilinx/<ip_name>_run_ooc.tcl (OOC synthesis runner), xilinx/<ip_name>_run_xpr.tcl (full implementation runner), and xilinx/<ip_name>_ooc.xdc (timing constraints).

Generate Quartus Project — Prompts for a device part number, then generates altera/<ip_name>_project.tcl and altera/<ip_name>.sdc.

Generate Altera Platform Designer Component — Exports altera/<ip_name>_hw.tcl for use in Quartus Platform Designer.

Generate Xilinx Vivado Component — Exports xilinx/component.xml and xilinx/xgui/<ip_name>_v*.tcl for use in the Vivado IP catalog.

Generate Documentation — Renders docs/<ip_name>_datasheet.md, a Markdown datasheet covering ports, generics, bus interfaces, and (if present) the linked register map. Same command run by scaffolding when ipcraft.generate.includeDocs is enabled.

docs.title: Scaffold Packs
docs.text:
Command Palette Editor Title IPCraft: Preview Template Output Yes Yes (.j2 files) IPCraft: Pin Preview IP Core Yes No IPCraft: Export Built-in Scaffold Pack Yes

Preview Template Output — Opens a read-only, live-refreshing preview of a .j2 template's rendered output next to the editor, evaluated against a pinned or auto-detected .ip.yml file. See Scaffold Packs.

Pin Preview IP Core — Chooses the .ip.yml file that supplies data for template previews until another file is pinned.

Export Built-in Scaffold Pack — Copies a built-in or example scaffold pack (and all its templates) into .vscode/ipcraft/packs/<name>/ in the workspace as a starting point for customization.

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
These commands are available on .ip.yml files.

Command Palette IPCraft Menu Editor Title IPCraft: Check Consistency Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Check HDL Consistency (managed:false) Yes Yes

Check Consistency — Cross-references the spec's declared ports, clocks, resets, generics, bus interfaces, and registers against the generated top-level HDL entity/module and, when scaffolded, the Platform Designer (_hw.tcl) and Vivado (component.xml) vendor artifacts. Reports drift in both directions: implementation-only items (extra port/parameter — a plausible adopt) and spec-only items (missing port/parameter — declared but gone from the implementation), plus property mismatches (direction/width/default) on items both sides declare.

Check HDL Consistency (managed:false) — The same cross-check restricted to the top-level HDL entity/module, regardless of the file's managed: flag.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
These commands are available on .ip.yml files and require vendor tools installed and reachable (see Settings below).

Command Palette IPCraft Menu Editor Title Status Bar IPCraft: Build Yes Yes Yes IPCraft: Build: Vivado OOC Synthesis Yes Yes IPCraft: Build: Quartus Compile Yes Yes IPCraft: Show Build Output Yes Yes Yes (click)

Build — Detects available build targets by checking for xilinx/<ip_name>_run_ooc.tcl, xilinx/<ip_name>_run_xpr.tcl, and altera/<ip_name>_project.tcl. When multiple targets exist, a QuickPick is shown. The selected tool runs in batch mode; output streams live to the IPCraft Build Output Channel. On completion, the IPCraft Build sidebar panel updates with parsed timing and utilization metrics.

Build: Vivado OOC Synthesis — Directly runs the Vivado OOC synthesis target without a QuickPick prompt.

Build: Quartus Compile — Directly runs the Quartus compile target without a QuickPick prompt.

Available build targets:

Target Tool Reports written to Vivado OOC Synthesis vivado -mode batch xilinx/build/ooc/ Vivado Full Implementation (XPR) vivado -mode batch xilinx/build/xpr/ Quartus Compile quartus_sh --flow compile altera/build/output_files/

Show Build Output — Opens the IPCraft Build Output Channel. The status bar item also triggers this command on click.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
Command Palette IPCraft Menu Editor Title IPCraft: Import from VHDL (Experimental) Yes Yes Yes (.vhd, .vhdl) IPCraft: Import from Altera Platform Designer (Experimental) Yes Yes Yes (_hw.tcl) IPCraft: Import from Xilinx Component XML (Experimental) Yes Yes Yes (component.xml)

Import from VHDL — Parses a .vhd or .vhdl file and extracts entity name, generics, clock/reset/port signals, and bus interfaces (AXI4-Full, AXI4-Lite, AXI-Stream, Avalon-MM, Avalon-ST). Creates <entity_name>.ip.yml in the same directory.

Import from Altera Platform Designer — Parses a _hw.tcl file (Altera IP specification language) and creates an .ip.yml spec.

Import from Xilinx Component XML — Parses a Vivado IP-XACT component.xml and creates .ip.yml. If register data is present (memory maps), a .mm.yml is also created.

Note: Import commands are experimental. Complex or non-standard files may not parse correctly.

docs.title: Vivado Integration
docs.text:
Command Palette IPCraft Menu Editor Title IPCraft: Edit in IP Packager Yes Yes (component.xml) IPCraft: Open in Platform Designer Yes Yes (_hw.tcl) IPCraft: Scan Vivado IP Catalog Yes IPCraft: Scan Vivado Interface Catalog Yes IPCraft: Open in Vivado Yes Yes Yes (.ip.yml) IPCraft: Open in Quartus Yes Yes Yes (.ip.yml) IPCraft: Select Vivado Version Yes (.xpr) Yes (.xpr) IPCraft: Select Quartus Version Yes (.qpf) Yes (.qpf)

Select Vivado Version / Select Quartus Version — With a Vivado .xpr or Quartus .qpf project open, choose which installed version opens and builds it, and pin that choice for the workspace (ipcraft.vivado.pinnedVersion / ipcraft.quartus.pinnedVersion).

Edit in IP Packager — Launches Vivado in GUI mode with the selected component.xml, opening it directly in the IP Packager. Requires Vivado to be configured (see ipcraft.vivado.runner and ipcraft.vivado.installDirs).

Open in Platform Designer — Launches Quartus Platform Designer (qsys-edit) with the selected _hw.tcl component. Requires Quartus to be configured (see ipcraft.quartus.runner and ipcraft.quartus.installDirs).

Scan Vivado IP Catalog — Invokes Vivado in batch mode to enumerate the installed IP catalog and caches the result in the IPCraft config directory. Used for bus-library suggestions.

Scan Vivado Interface Catalog — Invokes Vivado in batch mode to enumerate the installed bus/abstraction interface definitions and caches the result, so the canvas can suggest Vivado-native interface types.

Open in Vivado — Generates the Vivado project if it does not yet exist, then launches Vivado GUI pointing at the project. Prompts for a board/part if no default is configured.

Open in Quartus — Generates the Quartus project if it does not yet exist, then launches Quartus GUI pointing at the project. Prompts for a device if no default is configured.

docs.title: Browse
docs.text:
Command Palette Editor Title IPCraft: View Bus Definitions Yes IPCraft: Scan Workspace Bus Definitions Yes IPCraft: Copy Component Instance Yes Yes (.vhd, .vhdl, .v, .sv)

View Bus Definitions — Shows a QuickPick of the built-in bus definition YAML files (AXI4-Lite, AXI4, AXI-Stream, Avalon-MM, Avalon-ST, and custom definitions). Selecting one opens the file in a read-only editor.

Scan Workspace Bus Definitions — Re-scans the workspace for standalone bus/abstraction definition files (YAML files with a top-level ports array, or IP-XACT busDefinition/abstractionDefinition XML pairs) and refreshes the set of known interfaces available in the canvas Inspector.

Copy Component Instance — Copies a VHDL/Verilog instantiation template for the selected source file's entity/module to the clipboard.

docs.title: Walkthroughs
docs.text:
Command Palette IPCraft: Open Walkthrough... Yes IPCraft: Get Started with Scaffold Packs Yes IPCraft: Design Your First IP Core Yes IPCraft: IP Core with a Register Map Yes IPCraft: Bring Your VHDL into IPCraft Yes IPCraft: Import from Xilinx or Intel Tools Yes IPCraft: Synthesize and Check Timing Yes

Open Walkthrough... — Shows a QuickPick of all IPCraft walkthroughs. The other commands each jump directly to one.

docs.title: Editor Mode
docs.text:
Command Palette Editor Title IPCraft: Open as Text Editor Yes Yes (.ip.yml, .mm.yml) IPCraft: Open as Visual Editor Yes Yes (.ip.yml, .mm.yml) IPCraft: Preview in IPCraft (Experimental) Yes IPCraft: Open as System Diagram (fpga-ip-core.openSystemDiagram) Yes (system design files) Yes (system design files) IPCraft: Export Diagram as Image (fpga-ip-core.exportDiagramImage) Yes (IP core and system diagram editors) IPCraft: Compare System Design with... (fpga-ip-core.compareSystemDesign) Yes (system diagram editor)

Open as Text Editor — Reopens the current .ip.yml or .mm.yml file in the default VS Code text editor.

Open as Visual Editor — Reopens the current file in the IPCraft visual editor. Useful after opening a file with the text editor.

Preview in IPCraft — Opens a _hw.tcl, component.xml, VHDL, Verilog, or SystemVerilog file as a read-only IP core preview, from which you can save an .ip.yml. The same as Ctrl+Shift+V (Cmd+Shift+V) on those files. Experimental.

Compare System Design with... — Asks what to compare the open system diagram (the current side) with, as the base: another open design, HEAD, the merge base with the default branch, a commit that changed the file, a branch or tag, a typed revision, or another file, and lists the differences in the Changes tab of the bottom panel. The same as the Compare button in the toolbar. See Viewing a System Design.

Export Diagram as Image — Opens the export options of the active IP core editor or system diagram (the same popover as the camera button in the toolbar) to save the diagram as an SVG, PNG or JPG file. See Viewing a System Design.

Open as System Diagram — Opens a system design file in a read-only system diagram with hierarchy, details, and address map. Supported files are Vivado write_bd_tcl block design scripts (.tcl), Vivado block design files (.bd, Vivado 2018.3 and later), Platform Designer .qsys systems (Standard), and Platform Designer system scripts (qsys-script .tcl). The file is read statically and never executed. A _hw.tcl file keeps its own preview. See Viewing a System Design. Press Ctrl+Shift+V (Cmd+Shift+V on macOS) again to return to the text editor.

docs.title: Migrate
docs.text:
Command Palette IPCraft: Migrate Legacy IP Cores (vendor: → targets:) Yes

Migrate Legacy IP Cores — Scans the workspace for .ip.yml files that use the old vendor: field and rewrites them to the new targets: array format used by ipcraft.generate.targets.

docs.title: Help and settings
docs.text:
Command Palette Toolbar IPCraft: Open Extension Settings Yes Yes IPCraft: Report Issue / Send Feedback Yes Yes

Open Extension Settings filters VS Code Settings to IPCraft options.

Report Issue / Send Feedback opens the project's issue and feedback page.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Configure via File → Preferences → Settings and search for IPCraft, or edit settings.json directly.

docs.title: Vivado
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.vivado.runner "local" | "docker" "local" How IPCraft executes Vivado. local uses a native install; docker runs every command in a container. ipcraft.vivado.installDirs string[] [] (local) Vivado installation directories, one per version installed side by side (e.g. /tools/Xilinx/Vivado/2024.2). IPCraft detects each version and, for an existing project, uses the version it was created with. Leave empty to rely on vivado being in PATH. ipcraft.vivado.dockerImages object[] [] (docker) Docker images, one per version. Each entry needs label (the version shown in pickers) and image. ipcraft.vivado.pinnedVersion string "" Version or label to use in this workspace without detecting or asking. Also set by Select Vivado Version. ipcraft.vivado.installDir, ipcraft.vivado.dockerImage string "" Deprecated single-version forms of installDirs and dockerImages. ipcraft.vivado.defaultPart string "xc7z020clg484-1" Fallback FPGA part when no board has been selected. ipcraft.customBoards.vivado object[] [] Custom Vivado boards shown under My Boards in the board picker. Each entry requires label (string) and part (Xilinx part number). ipcraft.vivado.pinnedPart string "" Part chosen and pinned for the current workspace via the board picker; takes precedence over defaultPart when set. Written by the board picker, not usually edited by hand.

docs.title: Quartus
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.quartus.runner "local" | "docker" "local" How IPCraft executes Quartus. local uses a native install; docker runs every command in a container. ipcraft.quartus.installDirs string[] [] (local) Top-level Quartus installation directories, one per version (e.g. /opt/intelFPGA_pro/23.1). IPCraft locates quartus_sh and qsys-edit inside each and detects its version. ipcraft.quartus.dockerImages object[] [] (docker) Docker images, one per version. Each entry needs label and image. ipcraft.quartus.pinnedVersion string "" Version or label to use in this workspace without detecting or asking. Also set by Select Quartus Version. ipcraft.quartus.installDir, ipcraft.quartus.dockerImage string "" Deprecated single-version forms of installDirs and dockerImages. ipcraft.quartus.defaultDevice string "5CSEBA6U23I7" Fallback device part when no board has been selected. ipcraft.customBoards.quartus object[] [] Custom Quartus boards shown under My Boards in the board picker. Each entry requires label (string) and device (Intel/Altera part number). ipcraft.quartus.pinnedDevice string "" Device chosen and pinned for the current workspace via the board picker; takes precedence over defaultDevice when set. Written by the board picker, not usually edited by hand.

docs.title: Build
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.build.jobs number 4 Number of parallel jobs passed to Vivado launch_runs and Quartus compilation.

docs.title: GUI / X11
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.gui.display string "" DISPLAY environment variable to use for GUI tools (Vivado, Quartus, Platform Designer). Falls back to the process DISPLAY when unset. Useful for Remote SSH / X11 forwarding. ipcraft.gui.xauthority string "" XAUTHORITY environment variable to use for GUI tools, for X11 forwarding setups that need an explicit auth file.

docs.title: Generation
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.generate.targets string[] [] Synthesis vendor targets to include when scaffolding (e.g. ["vivado"], ["vivado","quartus"]). Empty array generates HDL and testbench only. ipcraft.generate.hdlLanguage "vhdl" | "systemverilog" "vhdl" HDL language for RTL file generation. ipcraft.generate.includeTestbench boolean true Include a testbench when scaffolding a project. ipcraft.generate.includeDocs boolean true Generate a Markdown IP datasheet (docs/<ip_name>_datasheet.md) when scaffolding a project. ipcraft.generate.scaffoldPack string "" Scaffold pack used for RTL/testbench generation. See Scaffold Packs.

docs.title: Testbench
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.testbench.framework "cocotb" | "vunit" "cocotb" Testbench framework. cocotb generates a Python/pytest test + Makefile; vunit generates a run.py + VHDL testbench entity. ipcraft.testbench.engine "ghdl" | "icarus" | "verilator" | "questa" "ghdl" Simulation engine used by the generated testbench.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.toolbar.targets string[] ["vivado","quartus"] Which vendor toolchain sections to display in the IP Core editor toolbar.

docs.title: Import
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.import.vendor string "user" Vendor name to assign when importing IP cores. "user" auto-detects from the git user.email domain. ipcraft.import.library string "ip" Default library name assigned when importing. ipcraft.import.version string "1.0.0" Default version string assigned when importing.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: Setting Type Default Description ipcraft.busLibraryPaths string[] [] Additional directories to search recursively for custom bus definition YAML files (.yml/.yaml). ipcraft.ipRepositoryPaths string[] [] Additional directories to scan for IP cores (directories containing .ip.yml or component.xml files). ipcraft.scaffoldPackPaths string[] [] Additional directories to scan recursively for custom Scaffold Packs. See Scaffold Packs.

docs.title: IPCraft Build Sidebar Panel
docs.text:
The IPCraft Build panel in the Explorer sidebar shows the result of the last IPCraft: Build invocation. It has four states:

State Display Idle No build yet — run IPCraft: Build Running Spinner with Building… Failed Error icon with Build failed — check Output Channel Success Expandable tree of timing and utilization results

When a build succeeds, the tree shows:

Vivado — OOC          PASS
├── Timing            PASS
│   ├── WNS +1.234 ns PASS
│   ├── WHS +0.456 ns PASS
│   └── Failing paths: 0
└── Utilization
    ├── LUT: 1,234 / 53,200 (2.3%)
    ├── FF:  2,891 / 106,400 (2.7%)
    └── BRAM: 4 / 140 (2.9%)

Clicking Timing or a CDC node opens the corresponding report file in the editor.

docs.title: Status Bar Item
docs.text:
The $(circuit-board) IPCraft item appears in the left status bar throughout the session.

State Display Idle $(circuit-board) IPCraft Building $(loading~spin) Building… Passed (Vivado) $(pass) WNS +1.23ns Passed (Quartus) $(pass) Fmax 156 MHz Failed $(error) Build failed (red background)

Clicking the item opens the IPCraft Build Output Channel.

docs.title: Generator Reference
docs.text:
IPCraft can generate HDL, tests, documentation, and files for Vivado or Quartus. The selected scaffold pack controls the exact file list and directory layout.

The commands that run the generator, and the staging review that shows every file before it is written, are described in Generating a project.

docs.title: Common output layout
docs.text:
A complete built-in pack may produce:

generated-core/
├── rtl/
│   ├── <name>_pkg.vhd
│   ├── <name>.vhd
│   ├── <name>_core.vhd
│   ├── <name>_<bus>.vhd
│   └── <name>_regs.vhd
├── tb/
│   ├── <name>_test.py
│   ├── test_<name>_sim.py
│   ├── register_model.py
│   ├── verification_manifest.json
│   └── Makefile
├── docs/
│   └── <name>_datasheet.md
├── xilinx/
│   ├── component.xml
│   └── ...
└── altera/
    ├── <name>_hw.tcl
    └── ...

SystemVerilog output uses .sv files and normally includes a package, top module, core module, bus wrapper, and register module.

Smaller packs intentionally produce fewer files. See scaffold packs.

docs.title: Cocotb verification source of truth
docs.text:
For generated cocotb tests, tb/verification_manifest.json replaces memmap.yml as the machine-readable test input. IPCraft derives the manifest once from the normalized memory-map model and records the origin of every kind of fact:

  • register layout, reset values, access types, and array bounds come from the specification;
  • readable and writable masks, write effects, reserved/unmapped read behavior, and hardware/software arbitration come from generator policy;
  • bus type, data width, and byte-enable support come from the resolved bus binding.

tb/register_model.py is the transport-independent scoreboard. The generated AXI4-Lite and Avalon-MM adapters drive that same model. The memmap.yml.j2 template remains available to scaffold packs as a driver/documentation projection, but generated cocotb tests neither load nor interpret it. It is therefore not a second verification oracle.

docs.title: Generation options
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning targets [] Vendor outputs such as vivado or quartus hdlLanguage vhdl vhdl or systemverilog includeVhdl true Include RTL files, in VHDL or SystemVerilog despite the name includeRegs true Include generated register logic includeTestbench true Include test files includeDocs true Include generated Markdown documentation includeVivadoProject false Include Vivado project and build scripts targetPart Setting value Vivado FPGA part includeQuartusProject false Include Quartus project files quartusDevice Setting value Quartus device part indentStyle, indentSize Pack or setting value Indentation of generated HDL, Tcl, XDC, and SDC files framework, engine Setting value Testbench framework (cocotb, vunit) and simulator

The IP Core toolbar writes the common choices to the current file or workspace settings. Commands may ask for a missing part or device.

docs.title: Vendor targets
docs.text:
Target Packaging output None HDL, tests, and documentation only vivado component.xml and Vivado XGUI metadata quartus Platform Designer _hw.tcl component Both Both vendor packages

Project creation is a separate choice. For example, Vivado packaging can be generated without creating an out-of-context synthesis project.

docs.title: Bus selection
docs.text:
The generator uses the memory-mapped interface linked through memoryMapRef. Supported built-in register wrappers include AXI4-Lite and Avalon Memory-Mapped.

Use a full interface identity when possible, such as ipcraft:busif:axi4_lite:1.0. IPCraft normalizes supported short names before choosing templates.

docs.title: Template data
docs.text:
Templates use Nunjucks and have a .j2 suffix. IPCraft searches the selected scaffold pack first, then the built-in template library.

Templates do not read the YAML directly. IPCraft first validates the IP core and its memory maps and converts them into one versioned object, so every template sees the same calculated values: resolved widths and parameters, the primary clock and reset with their polarity, the bus type and its expanded signals, registers sorted by address with their software and hardware access behavior, and the address width. Editor-only state such as rowId, selected cells, or unfinished drafts is never part of it. Templates should use these calculated values instead of interpreting raw access strings or bus aliases themselves.

Common template values:

Value Meaning name, display_name Core names suitable for files and headings is_systemverilog Whether SystemVerilog is selected bus_type Short bus name used by templates has_memory_mapped_slave Whether register-bus output is needed has_endian_swap Whether top-level endian reflow logic is needed registers Registers sorted by address bus_ports, user_ports Physical interface and standalone ports interrupt_ports Interrupt signals with resolved bus-interface and clock associations endian_swap_ports, endian_swap_widths Ports and fixed widths used by endian reflow logic generics Core parameters xgui_pages Parameter uiPage/uiGroup layout as a page-group-parameter tree, for the Vivado xGUI display_items The same layout flattened into Platform Designer add_display_item records clock_port, reset_port Primary clock and reset names

A scaffold pack can declare the template-data version it needs with apiVersion in scaffold.yml, for example ^1.0. IPCraft checks that range before rendering and rejects a pack that needs an incompatible version, instead of rendering files with missing values. A pack without apiVersion is accepted. The data contract does not guarantee that every generated file is valid for every tool: compile the output and run the relevant vendor tests before publishing a pack.

The versioned template-data schema is src/generator/contract/template_context.schema.json. Template variables use snake case by design; TypeScript and IPCraft schema properties use camel case. The current contract version is 1.5.0. Version 1.5.0 adds per-register write_fields, needs_write_branch and read_source, and register access is derived from field accesses when a register has fields. Version 1.3.0 adds display_items, display labels and Tcl-safe renderings for parameter metadata and defaults. Platform Designer group entries use stable internal IDs with their authored uiPage/uiGroup text in display_name; templates should not treat the ID as the visible label. Packs pinned to ~1.2 or an earlier minor must update their range after validating the additive parameter layout context; built-in packs use the compatible ^1.0 range.

docs.title: Testbench selection
docs.text:
Framework Supported simulator choices Main output Cocotb GHDL, Icarus Verilog, Verilator, Questa Python tests and simulator runner VUnit GHDL run.py and VHDL testbench

The framework controls how tests are written. The simulator choice controls how the generated HDL is compiled and run.

See Running a Cocotb simulation.

docs.title: Vendor build output
docs.text:
Vivado builds write reports under xilinx/build/; Quartus builds write output under altera/build/. IPCraft parses timing and resource-use reports for the Build view.

For commands, configuration, and report states, see Building a project.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: The ipcraft command runs the same generator outside VS Code. See Command line.

docs.title: Contributor implementation
docs.text: Implementation details belong in generator architecture. Source templates are under src/generator/templates/; copied files under dist/templates/ must not be edited.

docs.title: IP Core Editor Reference
docs.text:
The IP Core editor is the visual editor for .ip.yml files. It presents the core as a block with parameters, clocks, resets, ports, and bus interfaces.

VLNV means vendor, library, name, and version. It is the four-part identity shown in the toolbar.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Toolbar: identity, target, language, scaffold pack, actions       |
+----------------+-------------------------------+-----------------+
| Library        | IP block canvas               | Inspector       |
| palette        |                               |                 |
+----------------+-------------------------------+-----------------+
Area Purpose Toolbar Chooses generation options and starts project actions Library palette Supplies items that can be dragged onto the core Canvas Shows the core's public structure Inspector Edits the selected item

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
Controls are ordered from left to right:

Group Purpose History Undo or redo canvas changes Target Choose Vivado, Quartus, or both Language Choose VHDL or SystemVerilog Scaffold Template Choose the generated file structure Generate Generate the project, HDL, tests, documentation, or a register map Integration Generate, open, edit, or build vendor projects Consistency Compare the specification with generated files Utilities Open walkthroughs, settings, and feedback

Vendor actions remain disabled until their required project or component file exists. Hover over a control to see its name and any shortcut.

docs.title: Library palette
docs.text:
Category Items Parameters Integer, Boolean, and String parameters Infrastructure Clock, reset, interrupt, and individual port Bus protocols AXI, Avalon, streaming, and custom interfaces

Drag an item onto the canvas. IPCraft assigns an initial name; use the Inspector to change it.

docs.title: Canvas
docs.text:
• clocks, resets, and input ports appear on the left;
  • outputs and bidirectional ports appear on the right;
  • bus interfaces appear as bundles with a protocol and mode label;
  • parameters appear along the bottom;
  • interface arrays show their element count;
  • related interfaces use a shared clock-domain color.

Select the expand control on a bus bundle to see its individual signals.

docs.title: Canvas navigation
docs.text: Interaction Action Ctrl/Cmd + wheel Zoom Wheel Pan Middle-button drag Pan freely Space + background drag Pan freely Background drag Select several items Ctrl/Cmd + 0 Return to 100% zoom

docs.title: Export an image
docs.text:
Click Export image (the camera icon in the Utilities group), or run IPCraft: Export Diagram as Image, to save the block diagram as an SVG, PNG or JPG file. The popover offers the format, the Area (Current view is exactly the part of the symbol the canvas shows at the current zoom and pan; Whole diagram is the full symbol), the Scale (PNG and JPG, 1 to 4), the Theme (Light by default, or Dark), the Grid and the Background (editor or transparent; JPG is always opaque). The image is the symbol drawn with the bundled IBM Plex fonts: bus interfaces are always collapsed, and selection, hover, validation marks and the HUD are not drawn. It is the same picture that ipcraft render core.ip.yml writes. Exporting never changes the canvas view, and your last options are remembered for this workspace. The save dialog suggests <ip-name>.png next to the .ip.yml.

Current view needs every bus bundle collapsed on the canvas, because the image draws bundles collapsed and the layouts would differ. With a bundle expanded the export stops with a message; collapse the bundles, or export the Whole diagram.

docs.title: Inspector
docs.text:
The Inspector changes with the selection:

Selection Editable information Clock or reset Name and relationships Port Name, direction, and width Parameter Name, type, and default value Bus interface Name, mode, prefix, clock, reset, memory map, widths, and array count Expanded bus signal Signal width override

Widths may be numbers, parameter names, or supported arithmetic expressions.

docs.title: Keyboard commands
docs.text:
These commands work when no text box is being edited:

Key Action Delete Delete the selection Ctrl/Cmd + D Duplicate the selection Ctrl/Cmd + Z Undo Ctrl/Cmd + Y Redo Ctrl/Cmd + F Find a port Ctrl/Cmd + 0 Reset zoom Escape Close search or clear the selection

Dragging an item to the Remove Zone is another way to delete it.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The editor checks that clock, reset, and memory-map references point to existing items. Select a validation message to navigate to the affected canvas item.

Check Consistency performs a broader comparison with generated HDL and vendor files. See Checking consistency.

docs.title: Custom interfaces
docs.text:
Dragging Custom Interface creates a conduit: a named group of signals that does not use a built-in protocol. Add its signals in the Inspector. You can save the definition as a reusable .busdef.yml file.

See Custom interfaces.

docs.title: Generation review
docs.text:
Generation first opens a staging view. Review which files are new, changed, protected, or skipped before accepting the output.

The selected scaffold pack controls the output layout. See Generating a project and scaffold packs.

docs.title: Contributor implementation
docs.text:
The application entry is src/webview/ipcore/IpCoreApp.tsx. Canvas components are under src/webview/ipcore/components/canvas/, and state hooks are under src/webview/ipcore/hooks/.

The main responsibilities are:

Module Responsibility useIpCoreState Parsed core data, updates, and validation useIpCoreSync Versioned updates to the extension host useCanvasDrop Converts dropped palette items into model changes useCanvasSelection Current canvas selection useCanvasUndo Canvas history IpBlockCanvas Layout, rendering, and drop handling CanvasInspector Selection-specific forms StagingOverlay Generated-file review

See webview architecture for the process boundary and shared domain rules.

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcuts apply to the editor section that currently has focus. Text fields keep normal typing shortcuts unless a table cell is explicitly in navigation mode.

docs.title: Switching Editors
docs.text: Key Action Ctrl+Shift+V / Cmd+Shift+V On a Vivado block design .tcl script or .bd file, a Platform Designer .qsys file, or a Platform Designer system script, open the read-only system diagram; in the diagram, return to the text editor

docs.title: System Diagram
docs.text:
Key Action Left / Right With a panel separator focused, resize the outline or details panel by 16 px Up / Down With the bottom panel separator focused, resize it by 16 px + / - With the canvas focused in an isolated view, show the blocks one connection further (+ or =) or remove the outermost ring (-); ignored while typing and with Ctrl, Cmd or Alt held

Panels start hidden; open them with the toolbar toggles. Double-click a separator to collapse its panel again.

Double-click a block or port to zoom to it, or empty canvas to fit the level. Double-clicking a hierarchy block opens it. Its + button, or right-click and Expand In-Place, draws its inside in place instead; - or Collapse folds it again, and Open Subsystem in the same menu opens it.

docs.title: IP Core Canvas
docs.text:
These shortcuts are active when the canvas view is visible and no text field is focused.

Key Action Delete Delete the selected element (port, clock, reset, generic, or bus interface) Ctrl+D / Cmd+D Duplicate selected element; bus interfaces increment their array count instead of adding a copy Ctrl+Z / Cmd+Z Undo last canvas change (native VS Code document undo) Ctrl+Y / Cmd+Y Redo Ctrl+0 / Cmd+0 Reset zoom to 100 % Ctrl+F / Cmd+F Open port search (works even while another input is focused) Escape Close port search if open, otherwise deselect current element

docs.title: Canvas Navigation
docs.text: Interaction Action Ctrl+Wheel Zoom in / out Plain wheel Pan (vertical scroll; trackpads also pan horizontally on shift/2-axis scroll) Middle-mouse drag Pan freely Hold Space + left-button drag on background Pan freely Left-button drag on background (no Space) Marquee-select multiple ports/interrupts

docs.title: Register Fields Table
docs.text:
When the fields table is focused:

Key Action Arrow keys Navigate cells (row/column) h j k l Vim-style cell navigation F2 or e Enter edit mode on current cell Enter Save edit Escape Exit edit mode / return focus to table o Insert field after selected row O (Shift+O) Insert field before selected row d or Delete Delete selected field Alt+Up Move selected field up Alt+Down Move selected field down Tab Next cell Shift+Tab Previous cell

docs.title: Bit Field Visualizer (Pro Layout)
docs.text:
When a field in the visualizer has keyboard focus (Tab to it, or click then use the keys below):

Key Action Shift+Left / Shift+Right (horizontal layout) or Shift+Up / Shift+Down (vertical layout) Resize focused field by 1 bit Alt+Left / Alt+Right (horizontal layout) or Alt+Up / Alt+Down (vertical layout) Reorder focused field (swap with neighbor)

docs.title: Outline Sidebar
docs.text: Key Action Arrow keys or j / k Navigate tree items Enter / Space Toggle expand/collapse → or l Focus the details panel F2 or e Inline rename

docs.title: Shift + Pointer
docs.text: Target Action Existing field Resize (drag edge to expand/shrink) Gap (empty bits) Create new field (drag to select range)

docs.title: Ctrl/Cmd + Pointer
docs.text: Target Action Existing field Reorder (drag to new position, live preview)

docs.title: Adding fields with the mouse
docs.text:
Target Action Gap between table rows Hover to show the (+) bar, then click it to insert a 1-bit field. The bar appears only where a free bit exists next to the gap; fields are never shifted to make room. Field table row Right-click, then choose Insert Above or Insert Below Field in the visualizer Right-click, then choose Insert Before (toward lower bits) or Insert After (toward higher bits) Empty register Click the round (+) button

The new field's name is focused so you can type it right away. If the adjacent bit is occupied or outside the register, an error is shown and nothing changes.

docs.title: Reset Value Cells
docs.text: Interaction Action Click bit cell Toggle between 0 and 1 Drag across cells Set multiple bits to same value Type in hex bar Set register value directly

docs.title: Specification Schemas
docs.text:
IPCraft uses two YAML file types. JSON Schemas in the ipcraft-spec submodule define exactly which fields and values are valid.

File Describes *.ip.yml One IP core: identity, ports, parameters, interfaces, and source files *.mm.yml One or more memory maps: address blocks, registers, and fields

The tables below are a readable overview. The JSON Schema files remain the authoritative definition.

docs.title: Minimal IP core
docs.text:
VLNV means vendor, library, name, and version. Together these values identify a core without relying on its filename.

apiVersion: "1.0"
vlnv:
  vendor: example.org
  library: peripherals
  name: status_reader
  version: 1.0.0

description: Reads a status input

clocks:
  - name: clk

resets:
  - name: rst_n
    polarity: activeLow

ports:
  - name: status_i
    direction: in
    width: 8

Common top-level fields:

Field Meaning apiVersion Specification format version vlnv Vendor, library, name, and version description, author Human-readable ownership and purpose clocks, resets, interrupts, ports Individual signals parameters Configurable values used by widths or generation busInterfaces Named protocol interfaces memoryMaps Inline or referenced register maps subcores Other IP cores used by this one simulation Per-core test framework and simulator choices targets Vendor outputs such as vivado and quartus scaffold_pack Saved scaffold-pack selection fileSets Source files grouped by purpose

Interrupts may optionally name the memory-mapped slave and clock domain that serve them:

interrupts:
  - name: irq
    direction: out
    associatedBusInterface: control
    associatedClock: clk

associatedBusInterface references a memory-mapped slave in busInterfaces; associatedClock references an entry in clocks. Vendor generators translate these portable names to their native association properties.

docs.title: Bus interfaces
docs.text:
busInterfaces:
  - name: control
    type: ipcraft:busif:axi4_lite:1.0
    mode: slave
    physicalPrefix: s_axi
    associatedClock: clk
    associatedReset: rst_n
    memoryMapRef: control_map
Field Meaning name Interface name inside this core type Full bus identity or supported short name mode master, slave, source, sink, or conduit physicalPrefix Prefix used by physical HDL port names associatedClock, associatedReset Related clock and reset names memoryMapRef Linked memory map for memory-mapped interfaces array Count and naming rule for repeated interfaces useOptionalPorts Optional protocol signals to include absentPorts Required protocol signals intentionally missing from imported HDL portWidthOverrides Signal-specific width changes endianness Data byte order; for Avalon-ST, big places the first symbol in the most-significant data bits conduitPorts Inline signals for a custom interface

docs.title: Minimal memory map
docs.text:
A memory-map file contains a YAML list, even when it describes only one map:

- name: control_map
  addressBlocks:
    - name: control
      baseAddress: 0x0000
      range: 4K
      usage: register
      defaultRegWidth: 32
      registers:
        - name: CONTROL
          offset: 0x00
          fields:
            - name: ENABLE
              bits: "[0]"
              access: read-write
              resetValue: 0

docs.title: Address blocks
docs.text: Field Meaning name Block name baseAddress First address range Reserved size in bytes, including forms such as 4K usage register, memory, or reserved access Default software access defaultRegWidth Default register width in bits registers Registers and register arrays

docs.title: Registers
docs.text: Field Meaning name Register name offset Byte offset from the block base size Register width in bits access Default access inherited by fields resetValue Whole-register reset value fields Bit fields count, stride Repetition count and distance for an array registers Child registers in a repeated group

docs.title: Bit fields
docs.text:
A field may use bits, or the equivalent offset and width values. bits uses the highest bit first: "[7:4]" covers four bits.

Field Meaning name Field name bits Saved range such as "[7:0]" offset, width Lowest bit and number of bits access Read, write, or special write behavior resetValue Reset value limited to the field width enumeratedValues Names for known numeric values monitorChangeOf Field whose changes set this event field

docs.title: Bus library
docs.text:
Built-in definitions under ipcraft-spec/bus_definitions/ describe AXI4-Lite, AXI4, AXI Stream, Avalon Memory-Mapped, and Avalon Streaming signals.

Each definition states the logical signal name, direction, width, and whether the signal is required. The canvas uses it to display interfaces, and the generator uses it to create physical ports.

Custom .busdef.yml files use the same model. Point useBusLibrary at a custom library or let IPCraft discover definitions in the workspace.

docs.title: Validation in a text editor
docs.text:
The IPCraft visual editors validate these files automatically. For YAML text editing, install the Red Hat YAML extension and associate the schemas:

{
  "yaml.schemas": {
    "./ipcraft-spec/schemas/ip_core.schema.json": "*.ip.yml",
    "./ipcraft-spec/schemas/memory_map.schema.json": "*.mm.yml"
  }
}

docs.title: Schema and type changes
docs.text:
The schema sources are:

ipcraft-spec/schemas/ip_core.schema.json
ipcraft-spec/schemas/memory_map.schema.json
src/generator/contract/template_context.schema.json

After changing a schema:

npm run generate-types
npm run compile

Generated TypeScript files must not be edited by hand. Review the generated diff and compile it to find incompatible uses.

docs.title: Build and Verify a Scaffold Pack
docs.text:
This tutorial starts from a built-in scaffold pack, adds a generated Markdown file, and verifies the result.

You will learn how to:

  • export a pack into the workspace;
  • add one template and output rule;
  • preview the generated file tree;
  • generate and compile the project.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• IPCraft installed or running in an Extension Development Host
  • a workspace containing an .ip.yml file
  • GHDL for VHDL verification, or Icarus Verilog for SystemVerilog

If you need a sample core, first follow Creating your first IP core.

docs.title: 1. Export a starting pack
docs.text:
1. Open the Command Palette.
  2. Run IPCraft: Export Built-in Scaffold Pack.
  3. Select builtin-ipcraft.
  4. Name the copy ipcraft-with-docs.

IPCraft creates:

.vscode/ipcraft/packs/ipcraft-with-docs/
├── scaffold.yml
└── ... copied templates

Open scaffold.yml. The Scaffold Pack Preview shows which files the selected IP core would generate.

docs.title: 2. Add a documentation template
docs.text:
Create .vscode/ipcraft/packs/ipcraft-with-docs/registers.md.j2:

# {{ display_name }} Register Map

{% if description %}{{ description }}{% endif %}

{% for register in registers %}
## {{ register.name }}

Offset: `{{ register.offset }}`

| Field | Bits | Access | Reset |
|---|---:|---|---:|
{% for field in register.fields %}
| `{{ field.name }}` | `{{ field.bits }}` | {{ field.access }} | `{{ field.resetValue }}` |
{% endfor %}

{% endfor %}

Template variable names in Nunjucks may use snake case. TypeScript and schema properties elsewhere in IPCraft use camel case.

docs.title: 3. Add an output rule
docs.text:
Append this entry to files in scaffold.yml:

  - source: "registers.md.j2"
    target: "docs/{{ name }}-registers.md"
    condition: "has_memory_mapped_slave"

The condition skips the file when the IP core has no memory-mapped slave interface.

To let users edit the generated document without later replacement, add:

    managed: false

A file with managed: false is created once and then treated as user-owned.

docs.title: 4. Preview before generation
docs.text:
Open registers.md.j2 and run IPCraft: Preview Template Output. If the workspace contains several IP cores, choose the one to use as preview data.

Also check the Scaffold Pack Preview beside scaffold.yml. The new file should appear as generated. If it appears as skipped, confirm that the selected core has a memory-mapped slave.

The two previews answer different questions:

Preview What to check Template output The contents of one rendered file Scaffold Pack Preview Output paths, conditions, and protected files

docs.title: 5. Select and generate
docs.text:
1. Open the IP core in the visual editor.
  2. Select ipcraft-with-docs from Scaffold Template.
  3. Run IPCraft: Scaffold Project (RTL + EDA packaging + Testbench).
  4. Review the staged file list.
  5. Accept the output.

The project should now contain a file similar to:

docs/<core-name>-registers.md

Open it and confirm that register names, offsets, fields, access, and reset values match the linked memory map.

docs.title: 6. Compile the generated HDL
docs.text:
Use the build command supplied by the generated project, or run the relevant HDL integration test in the IPCraft repository:

npm run test:integration:hdl

The Markdown file can look correct even when another template produces invalid HDL, so both checks matter.

docs.title: 7. Test regeneration behavior
docs.text:
Change a description in the source YAML and generate again.

  • With the default managed: true, the Markdown output should show the new description in the staging review.
  • With managed: false, an existing Markdown file should remain unchanged.

This verifies that the pack's ownership rule matches your intent.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Problem Likely cause Template is missing source does not match the .j2 filename Documentation file is skipped has_memory_mapped_slave is false Output path is unexpected target uses the wrong template value Preview uses another core Pin the intended file with IPCraft: Pin Preview IP Core Hand edits disappear Set managed: false for user-owned output Pack is not listed Check .vscode/ipcraft/packs/<name>/scaffold.yml

docs.title: What to do next
docs.text:
• Add only the templates your organization needs to change.
  • Keep conditions short and visible in the file-tree preview.
  • Generate both HDL languages if the pack claims to support both.
  • Run vendor integration tests when the pack creates Vivado or Quartus files.

See Customizing generated files with scaffold packs for the manifest and template-value reference.

docs.title: DE10-Nano Register-Map Case Study
docs.text: This case study shows where IPCraft fits in a complete Terasic DE10-Nano project. The maintained board files, build scripts, shared scenarios, and hardware results live with the generated designs under examples/.

docs.title: System path
docs.text:
The example register map contains:

  • read/write control fields;
  • read-only hardware status;
  • an event flag that software clears by writing 1;
  • hand-written application logic protected from regeneration.

docs.title: Verification stages
docs.text:
Stage What it proves Generate The YAML inputs produce RTL, tests, and Quartus metadata Simulate Reset, reads, writes, and event clearing behave as specified Compile Quartus accepts the generated project and reports timing and size Integrate Platform Designer connects the peripheral to the system bus Run on board Software reaches the same registers through the real interconnect

Each stage finds a different class of problem. Simulation can validate register behavior, but only the board run proves that addresses, interconnect, clocks, reset, firmware, and generated hardware work together.

docs.title: Repository boundary
docs.text:
IPCraft owns the path from the IP description to generated component files:

  • YAML validation;
  • RTL and register logic generation;
  • Cocotb test scaffolding;
  • Quartus component metadata;
  • headless project creation and builds.

This repository also owns the DE10-Nano harness used to regress those generated files:

  • pin assignments and clocks specific to the DE10-Nano;
  • the surrounding Platform Designer system;
  • programming and System Console transport scripts;
  • the manifest-driven hardware result.

This is a deliberate change from the earlier split with cvsoc. The conformance examples were moved into this repository so their generated manifest, semantic scoreboard, simulation scenarios, board build, and retained hardware evidence advance together. cvsoc remains the home for complete SoC applications; the board harness here is narrowly a generator verification target.

The shared contract is:

  • tb/verification_manifest.json describes the generated register semantics;
  • tb/register_model.py is the transport-independent expected-value model;
  • tb/conformance_scenarios.py contains the transactions used by simulation and hardware;
  • cocotb supplies the simulation Avalon-MM transport;
  • altera/debug/hardware_runner.py supplies the JTAG-to-Avalon transport and writes a machine-readable provenance result.

docs.title: Reproduce the IPCraft portion
docs.text:
You do not need the board to repeat the first three stages:

  1. Create an IP core and memory map.
  2. Generate the project.
  3. Run the generated simulation.
  4. If Quartus is available, run a headless build.

For the board-specific stages, use examples/regmap_conformance_avmm/:

cd examples/regmap_conformance_avmm/altera
make processor             # niosv on Quartus 24.x/25.x; nios2 on a legacy install
make qsys project compile
# Legacy flow: make PROCESSOR=nios2 USE_DOCKER=1 qsys project compile

The platform-specific hardware test target programs a fresh bitstream, verifies the manifest-derived build ID, runs the same directed and seeded-random scenarios as cocotb, and writes output_files/hardware-result.json. Missing Quartus tools, JTAG services, or the board produce a nonzero exit; they are never treated as a passing hardware run.

examples/regmap_conformance_axil/ proves the same register map and manifest-driven suite through the AXI4-Lite bus wrapper instead, over the same JTAG-to-Avalon-MM master bridged to AXI4 by Platform Designer -- same make qsys project compile && make test workflow, no HPS/Nios II required.

docs.title: Memory-Mapped Registers
docs.text:
This tutorial creates a small register map and explains how software-visible registers become generated hardware.

You will define:

  • one address block;
  • a control register that software can write;
  • a status register that software can read;
  • an interrupt flag cleared by writing 1.

docs.title: The basic idea
docs.text:
A processor reads and writes numbered addresses. The register map gives those addresses names and divides each register into fields.

For example, software may write address 0x00 to enable a device and read address 0x04 to check whether it is busy.

docs.title: Create the memory map
docs.text:
1. Open the Command Palette.
  2. Run IPCraft: New Register Map.
  3. Choose a file name such as daq_controller.mm.yml.
  4. Open the file in the Memory Map editor.

The editor follows this hierarchy:

docs.title: Add an address block
docs.text:
An address block is a continuous address range served by one interface.

Create a block named control with:

Property Value Meaning Base address 0x0000 First address in the block Range 0x1000 Total reserved address space Width 32 Bits transferred in one register word Usage register The block contains registers

The range can be larger than the registers currently defined. This leaves room for later versions without moving existing addresses.

docs.title: Add a control register
docs.text:
Add a register named CONTROL at offset 0x00. An offset is the register's position relative to the block's base address.

Add these fields:

Field Bits Software access Reset Purpose ENABLE 0 Read/write 0 Enable the device MODE 2:1 Read/write 0 Select an operating mode START 3 Write-only 0 Start one operation

To add a field, hover between two rows and click the (+) button, right-click a field and choose Insert Above or Insert Below, or press o with the table focused.

Bit ranges are written from the highest bit to the lowest bit. 2:1 therefore covers two bits.

The remaining bits are unused. Gaps are valid and remain visible in the bit field visualizer.
